Surah 43, al-Zukhruf, is Meccan by consensus. Muqatil said: except His words ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾ [43:45]. It has eighty-nine verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Ha Mim (1). By the Manifest Book (2), indeed We made it an Arabic Qur'an that you may understand (3).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Ha Mim. By the Manifest Book﴾. The discussion of this has already preceded [see vol. 15, p. 289]. It has been said: "Ha Mim" is an oath, and "By the Manifest Book" is a second oath, and Allah may swear by whatever He wills. The answer [to the oath] is "indeed We made it." Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever makes the answer to "By the Book" to be "Ha Mim" (as you say, "He descended, by Allah," "It is obligatory, by Allah") pauses at "the Manifest Book." Whoever makes the answer to the oath "indeed We made it" does not pause at "the Manifest Book." The meaning of "We made it" is that We named it and described it, and for this reason it takes two objects, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah did not make of any bahirah﴾ [5:103]. As-Suddi said: meaning We sent it down as a Qur'an. Mujahid said: We spoke it. Al-Zajjaj and Sufyan al-Thawri said: We made it clear. "Arabic" means We sent it down in the tongue of the Arabs, because every prophet had his book sent down in the language of his people; this was said by Sufyan al-Thawri and others. Muqatil said: because the language of the people of heaven is Arabic. It has also been said: the intended "Book" is all the books sent down upon the prophets, since "Book" is a generic noun, so it is as if He swore by all the books sent down that He made the Qur'an Arabic. The pronoun in His saying "We made it" refers to the Qur'an, even though it has not been mentioned in this surah, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed We sent it down in the Night of Decree﴾ [97:1] [see vol. 20, p. 129]. "That you may understand" means that you may comprehend its rulings and meanings. On this view, it is specific to the Arabs and not the non-Arabs, as said by Ibn Isa. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is "that you may reflect," and on this view the address is general to the Arabs and non-Arabs. He described the Book as "the Manifest" because Allah made clear in it its rulings and obligations, as has preceded in more than one place.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 4:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book﴾ meaning the Qur'an, in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), "with Us" (ladayna), "[it is] exalted and wise" (la'aliyyun hakim), i.e., lofty and firmly structured, in which there is no discrepancy or contradiction. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an, in a Book well-guarded﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 77-78]. And He, the Exalted, said: "Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a Preserved Tablet" [al-Buruj: 21-22].

Ibn Jurayj said: The meaning of His saying, may He be exalted, "And indeed it" (wa-innahu), i.e., the deeds of creation, of faith and disbelief, obedience and disobedience. "Exalted" (la'aliyyun) means lofty, too high to be reached so as to be altered. "Wise" (hakim) means protected from deficiency or alteration.

Ibn Abbas said: The first thing Allah created was the pen, and He commanded it to write what He intended to create. So the Book is with Him. Then he recited: "And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book, with Us, exalted and wise."

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read the hamza in "Umm al-Kitab" with a kasra (Ummi), while the rest read it with a damma (Umma). This has been discussed previously.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 5:

أَفَنَضْرِبُ عَنْكُمُ الذِّكْرَ صَفْحاً أَنْ كُنْتُمْ قَوْماً مُسْرِفِينَ (٥) قَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿أَفَنَضْرِبُ عَنْكُمُ الذِّكْرَ صَفْحاً﴾ يَعْنِي: الْقُرْآنَ، عَنِ الضَّحَّاكِ وَغَيْرِهِ.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Shall We then turn away the Reminder from you, altogether, because you are a people who transgress?﴾ He means: the Qur'an, according to al-Dahhak and others.

وَقِيلَ: الْمُرَادُ بِالذِّكْرِ الْعَذَابُ، أَيْ أَفَنَضْرِبُ عَنْكُمُ الْعَذَابَ [[ما بين المربعين ساقط من ل]] وَلَا نُعَاقِبُكُمْ عَلَى إِسْرَافِكُمْ وَكُفْرِكُمْ، قَالَهُ مُجَاهِدٌ وَأَبُو صَالِحٍ وَالسُّدِّيُّ، وَرَوَاهُ الْعَوْفِيُّ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ.

It is also said: the Reminder means the punishment, i.e., "Shall We then turn away the punishment from you [[what is between the brackets is missing in L]] and not punish you for your transgression and your disbelief?" This was said by Mujahid, Abu Salih and al-Suddi, and al-Awfi narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

وَقَالَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ: الْمَعْنَى أَفَحَسِبْتُمْ أَنْ نَصْفَحَ عَنْكُمُ الْعَذَابَ وَلَّمَا تَفْعَلُوا مَا أُمِرْتُمْ بِهِ.

Ibn Abbas said: the meaning is, "Do you think that We will turn away the punishment from you when you have not done what you were commanded?"

وَعَنْهُ أَيْضًا أَنَّ الْمَعْنَى أَتُكَذِّبُونَ بِالْقُرْآنِ وَلَا تُعَاقَبُونَ.

It is also narrated from him that the meaning is, "Do you deny the Qur'an and not be punished?"

وَقَالَ السُّدِّيُّ أَيْضًا: الْمَعْنَى أَفَنَتْرُكُكُمْ سُدًى فَلَا نَأْمُرُكُمْ وَلَا نَنْهَاكُمْ.

al-Suddi also said: the meaning is, "Shall We leave you aimless, so that We do not command you and do not forbid you?"

وَقَالَ قَتَادَةُ: الْمَعْنَى أَفَنُهْلِكُكُمْ وَلَا نَأْمُرُكُمْ وَلَا نَنْهَاكُمْ.

Qatadah said: the meaning is, "Shall We destroy you, and not command you and not forbid you?"

وَعَنْهُ أَيْضًا: أَفَنُمْسِكُ عَنْ إِنْزَالِ الْقُرْآنِ مِنْ قَبْلِ أَنَّكُمْ لَا تُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ فَلَا نُنَزِّلُهُ عَلَيْكُمْ. وَقَالَهُ ابْنُ زَيْدٍ.

It is also narrated from him: "Shall We withhold the sending down of the Qur'an because you do not believe in it, so that We do not send it down to you?" Ibn Zayd also said this.

قَالَ قَتَادَةُ: وَاللَّهِ لَوْ كَانَ هَذَا الْقُرْآنُ رُفِعَ حِينَ رَدَّدَتْهُ أَوَائِلُ هَذِهِ الْأُمَّةِ لَهَلَكُوا، وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَدَّدَهُ وَكَرَّرَهُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِرَحْمَتِهِ.

Qatadah said: By Allah, if this Qur'an had been lifted when the earliest of this community repeated it, they would have perished. But Allah, in His mercy, repeated it and reiterated it to them.

وَقَالَ الْكِسَائِيُّ: أَفَنَطْوِي عَنْكُمُ الذِّكْرَ طَيًّا فَلَا تُوعَظُونَ وَلَا تُؤْمَرُونَ.

al-Kisa'i said: "Shall We fold up the Reminder from you, folding it up, so that you are not admonished and not commanded?"

وَقِيلَ: الذِّكْرُ التَّذَكُّرُ، فَكَأَنَّهُ قَالَ أَنَتْرُكُ تَذْكِيرَكُمْ لِأَنْ كُنْتُمْ قَوْمًا مُسْرِفِينَ، فِي قِرَاءَةِ مَنْ فَتَحَ.

It is also said: "the Reminder" means the act of reminding, as if He said, "Shall We abandon reminding you because you are a people who transgress?" This is according to the reading of the one who opened the hamzah (i.e., read أَنْ with a fatḥah).

وَمَنْ كَسَرَ جعلها للشرط وَمَا قَبْلَهَا جَوَابًا لَهَا، لِأَنَّهَا لَمْ تَعْمَلْ فِي اللَّفْظِ. وَنَظِيرُهُ: ﴿وَذَرُوا مَا بَقِيَ مِنَ الرِّبا إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾[[آية ٢٧٨ سورة البقرة.]] [البقرة: ٢٧٨]

Whoever read it with a kasrah (إِنْ) made it a conditional particle, and what precedes it serves as its answer, because it does not govern anything in the wording. A parallel to this is: ﴿And leave what remains of interest, if you are believers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:278]. [[Verse 278 of surat al-Baqarah.]]

وَقِيلَ: الْجَوَابُ مَحْذُوفٌ دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ مَا تَقَدَّمَ، كَمَا تَقُولُ: أَنْتَ ظَالِمٌ إِنْ فَعَلْتَ.

It is also said: the answer is omitted, and what came before it indicates it, just as you say, "You are a wrongdoer if you do it."

وَمَعْنَى الْكَسْرِ عِنْدَ الزَّجَّاجِ الْحَالُ، لِأَنَّ فِي الْكَلَامِ مَعْنَى التَّقْرِيرِ وَالتَّوْبِيخِ.

According to al-Zajjaj, the meaning of the kasrah is the state (ḥal, i.e., "while"), because the sentence carries the sense of confirmation and rebuke.

وَمَعْنَى "صَفْحاً" إِعْرَاضًا، يُقَالُ: صَفَحْتُ عَنْ فُلَانٍ إِذَا أَعْرَضْتُ عَنْ ذَنْبِهِ. وَقَدْ ضَرَبْتُ عَنْهُ صَفْحًا إِذَا أَعْرَضْتُ عَنْهُ وَتَرَكْتُهُ.

The meaning of "ṣafḥan" is turning away. It is said: "I forgave so-and-so" (ṣafaḥtu ʿan fulānin) when I overlooked his sin; and "I turned away from him altogether" (ḍarabtu ʿanhu ṣafḥan) when I turned away from him and left him.

وَالْأَصْلُ فِيهِ صَفْحَةُ الْعُنُقِ، يُقَالُ: أَعْرَضْتُ عَنْهُ أَيْ وَلَّيْتُهُ صَفْحَةَ عُنُقِي. قَالَ الشَّاعِرُ [[هو كثير عزة.]]:

The root of this is the side of the neck: one says, "I turned away from him," meaning I presented to him the side of my neck. The poet said [[He is Kuthayyir ʿAzzah.]]:

صُفُوحًا فَمَا تَلْقَاكَ إِلَّا بَخِيلَةً ... فَمَنْ مَلَّ مِنْهَا ذَلِكَ الْوَصْلَ مَلَّتِ

"Forgiving often, yet you meet only a stingy beloved; whoever wearies of her such union, she too wearies of it."

وَانْتَصَبَ "صَفْحاً" عَلَى الْمَصْدَرِ لِأَنَّ مَعْنَى "أَفَنَضْرِبُ" أَفَنَصْفَحُ. وَقِيلَ: التَّقْدِيرُ أَفَنَضْرِبُ عَنْكُمُ الذِّكْرَ صَافِحِينَ، كَمَا يُقَالُ: جَاءَ فُلَانٌ مَشْيًا.

"Ṣafḥan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because the meaning of "afanaḍribu" is "afanaṣfaḥu" (shall We forgive). It is also said the implied sense is "Shall We turn the Reminder away from you while turning aside," as one says, "So-and-so came walking" (jāʾa fulānun mashyan).

وَمَعْنَى "مُسْرِفِينَ" مُشْرِكِينَ.

The meaning of "musrifīn" is "associators" (mushrikīn).

وَاخْتَارَ أَبُو عُبَيْدَةَ الْفَتْحَ فِي "أَنْ" وَهِيَ قِرَاءَةُ ابْنِ كَثِيرٍ وَأَبِي عَمْرٍو وَعَاصِمٍ وَابْنِ عَامِرٍ، قَالَ: لِأَنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى عَاتَبَهُمْ عَلَى مَا كَانَ منهم، وعلمه قبل ذلك من فعلهم.

Abu ʿUbaydah preferred the fatḥah on "an," and it is the reading of Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim and Ibn ʿAmir. He said: because Allah, may He be exalted, rebuked them for what had occurred from them, and He had known of their deeds beforehand.

How many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples? (Q. 43:6)

"Kam" here is khabariyyah (used to state a fact), and its purpose is to express abundance; the meaning is: how many prophets did We send! Like His saying: ﴿How many gardens and springs they left behind!﴾ (Q. 44:25), i.e., how much they left behind. "And no prophet came to them" means that no prophet came to them "but they mocked him," like the mockery of your people toward you. He consoles His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and comforts him. (Q. 43:7)

"So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might" means: a people stronger than them in power. The pronoun in "them" refers to the polytheists addressed in His saying: "Shall We withhold the Reminder from you and turn away, because you are a wasteful people?" So He referred to them by pronoun after addressing them. "Stronger" (ashadd) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It was also said that it is an object (maf'ul), meaning: We destroyed those who were stronger than these polytheists in their bodies and their followers. (Q. 43:8)

"And the example of the earlier peoples has passed" means: their punishment, related from Qatadah. It was also said that it is a description of "the earlier peoples," so He informs them that they were destroyed for their disbelief, as related by al-Naqqash and al-Mahdawi. The "mathal" (example) means description and report.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if you were to ask them﴾, meaning the polytheists, ﴿"Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Mighty, the All-Knowing"﴾. So they acknowledged to Him creation and origination, and then, out of ignorance, they worshipped others alongside Him. This has already been discussed in more than one place.[[See vol. 6, p. 384 and what follows.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 10:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who made the earth for you a cradle﴾. He described Himself, glory be to Him, with perfect power. This is the beginning of His giving information about Himself. Had this been a report of the words of the disbelievers, He would have said: "Who made the earth for us." "Mihadan" means a bed and a spread-out carpet. This has already been discussed [[see vol. 11, p. 209]]. The Kufans read "mahdan." ﴿And made for you therein roads﴾, i.e., means of livelihood. It was also said: roads, so that you may travel along them to wherever you wish. ﴿So that you may be guided﴾, meaning that you may infer from His created things His power. It was also said that "la'allakum tahtadun" means you may be guided on your journeys; this was said by Ibn 'Isa. It was also said: so that you may recognize the blessing of Allah upon you; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It was also said: you may be guided to your livelihoods.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 11:

Allah's words: ﴿And He who sends down water from the sky in a measure﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: That is, not as it was sent down upon the people of Nuh without measure, until it drowned them; rather, it is in a measure, neither a flood that drowns nor insufficient for the need, so that it becomes a means of livelihood for you and your cattle. ﴿So We revive thereby a dead land﴾: that is, We gave it life. ﴿Thereby﴾: that is, by the water. ﴿A dead land﴾: that is, barren of vegetation. ﴿Thus you will be brought forth﴾: that is, from your graves, because the One who is able to do this is able to do that. This has already been discussed in detail in (surah) al-A'raf. [[See vol. 7, p. (230)]]

Yahya ibn Waththab, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Dhakwan on the authority of Ibn 'Amir recited "yakhrujun" with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the ra'. The rest recited it in the passive form (the verb in the passive voice).

There are five issues in this passage.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He who created the pairs﴾, meaning: and Allah is the One who created the pairs. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it means all the kinds (al-asnaf). Al-Hasan said: the winter and the summer, the night and the day, the heavens and the earth, the sun and the moon, and Paradise and the Fire. It was also said: the pairs of animals, male and female; this was stated by Ibn 'Isa. It was also said: he intends the pairs of plants, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿And We caused to grow in it every beautiful pair﴾ [Qaf: 7][[Verse 7, Surah Qaf.]] and "every noble pair" [Luqman: 10]. It was also said: what a person turns over in of good and evil, faith and disbelief, benefit and harm, poverty and wealth, health and sickness. I say: this view encompasses all the other views and gathers them by its generality. "And He has made for you of the ships" (al-fulk), the ships, "and of the livestock" (al-an'am), the camels, "that which you ride" on land and sea. "That you may sit upon their backs" (zuhurihi). He used the pronoun in the singular because it refers back to what is in His saying "that which you ride." Abu 'Ubayd said this. Al-Farra' said: he attributed the backs (al-zuhur) to a singular because the intended sense is the genus, so the singular carries the meaning of the plural, like the words al-jaysh (army) and al-jund (troops). For this reason it was masculine, and he made "the backs" plural, meaning: upon the backs of this genus.

The second: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: al-an'am here means the camels and the cattle. Abu Mu'adh said: the camels alone, and this is the correct view, due to his peace be upon him saying: "While a man was riding a cow, it said to him: 'I was not created for this; I was created only for plowing.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'I believe in this, I and Abu Bakr and 'Umar.'" [Abu Bakr and 'Umar were not present among the people.] This has been discussed fully at the beginning of Surah al-Nahl [See vol. 10, p. 72], and praise be to Allah.

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that you may sit upon their backs﴾ is intended to refer specifically to the camels, by the evidence we have mentioned. Also, the ships are only ridden in their hulls (butun), but He mentioned both together at the beginning of the verse and linked the last of them to one of them. It may be understood that their outward (zahir) is their inward (batin), because the water covers and conceals them, and their inward is their outward, because it is exposed to those who see and becomes apparent to those who observe.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you may remember the favor of your Lord when you have settled upon them﴾, meaning: when you have mounted them. Remembering the favor is praising Allah for subjecting these to us on land and sea. "And say: Exalted is He who has subjected this to us," meaning: He has made this mount tame for us. In the recitation of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib it is: "Exalted is He who has subjected this to us." "And we could not have it under control" (muqrinin), meaning: capable of it, according to the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi. Al-Akhfash and Abu 'Ubayda said: muqrinin means controlling, restraining. It was also said: equal in strength and power, from their saying: "He is the qirn of so-and-so" when he is his equal in strength. It is said: "So-and-so is muqrin to so-and-so," meaning he controls him. "I aqrantu kadha" means I was able to do it, and "aqran lahu" means he was able to it and was strong enough for it, as if he became its equal. Allah, exalted is He, said: "And we could not have it under control" (muqrinin), meaning capable of it. Qutrub recited the verse of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib:

"The tribes know well that 'Uqayl
is, in calamities, among those who control us" [translation of: لَنَا فِي النَّائِبَاتِ بِمُقْرِنِينَا]

Another poet said:

"You have ridden my difficult she-camel in wickedness and injustice,
and you are not able to control the difficult ones."

Al-muqrin also means one whose neglect has overwhelmed him: he has camels or sheep and no helper to manage them, or he waters his camels and has no one to drive them away. Ibn al-Sikkit said: regarding its origin there are two views. The first: it is derived from iqran, one says "aqrana yuqrinu iqranan" when one is able to do something; "aqrantu kadha" means I was able to it and I controlled it, as if he put it into a qirn, which is a rope, and bound it and tied it firmly. The second: it is derived from muqaranah, which is that some of them are linked to others in travel. One says: "qaranta kadha bi-kadha" when you tie one thing to another and make it its companion.

The fifth: Allah, glorified is He, taught us what to say when we ride beasts, and He made known in another verse, on the tongue of Noah, peace be upon him, what to say when we ride ships, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he said: Board it; in the name of Allah is its course and its anchoring. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Hud: 41][[Verse 41, Surah Hud.]]. How many a rider of a beast has been thrown by it, or has bolted, or has been hurled onto its face, or has fallen from its back and perished? And how many who rode in a ship were drowned when it broke apart with them. Since riding is a direct matter, a forbidden matter, and a connection to causes of destruction, he is commanded not to forget, when he is connected to it, his day and that he is certainly perishing and will therefore return to Allah, exalted and mighty is He, unable to escape His decree. He should not leave the remembrance of this in his heart and tongue, until he is prepared to meet Allah by reforming himself. Beware that his riding should be among the causes of his death in Allah's knowledge while he is heedless of it. Sulayman ibn Yasar reported that a group were on a journey, and whenever they mounted they said: "Exalted is He who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it under control." Among them was a man on his she-camel that was razim, meaning one that does not move from weakness [A note written in the margin of a copy of the source, in the hand of its copyist: "The razim of camels: the one that stays fixed on the ground and does not rise from weakness. The she-camel razamat, yarzumu and yarzimu, razum and ruzam, when she stands from exhaustion and weakness and does not move, so she is razim. Said by al-Jawhari in al-Sihah."], and he said: "As for me, indeed I am able to control this one." He said: so she kicked him, and his neck was broken. It is also reported that a Bedouin rode his young camel and said: "Indeed I am able to control it," so the young camel kicked him until she threw him down, and his neck was broken. Al-Mawardi mentioned the first and Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned the second. He said: a servant should not abandon saying this, though it is not obligatory to mention it by tongue. So he says whenever he rides, especially when traveling, if he remembers: "Exalted is He who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it under control. And indeed to our Lord we are returning." O Allah, You are the companion on the journey and the successor over the family and property. O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the hardship of travel, the sorrow of returning, the injustice after the union, and the evil sight regarding family and property. By "the injustice after the union" he means the scattering of a man's affairs after they were gathered. 'Amr ibn Dinar said: I rode with Abu Ja'far to a land of his, near a garden called Mudrika, and he mounted a difficult camel. I said to him: "Abu Ja'far! Are you not afraid it will throw you?" He said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "On the hump of every camel is a devil; when you ride them, mention the name of Allah as He commanded you, then make them serve you, for Allah carries them." 'Ali ibn Rabi'a said: I witnessed 'Ali ibn Abi Talib ride a beast one day. When he placed his foot in the stirrup, he said: "In the name of Allah." When he settled on the beast, he said: "Praise be to Allah." Then he said: "Exalted is He who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it under control. And indeed to our Lord we are returning." Then he said: "Praise be to Allah, and Allah is greatest" three times, "O Allah, there is no god but You; I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You." Then he laughed. I said to him: "What made you laugh?" He said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ do as I did, and say as I said, then he laughed. I said: 'What makes you laugh, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'The servant, or he said: wonder at a servant who says: O Allah, there is no god but You; I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You, knowing that no one else forgives sins.'" Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi recorded it in his Musnad, and Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Khuwaiz Mandad in his Ahkam. Al-Tha'labi mentioned something similar in summary from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and his wording from him is: that the Prophet ﷺ, when he placed his foot in the stirrup, said: "In the name of Allah." When he settled, he said: "Praise be to Allah for every state. Exalted is He who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it under control, and indeed to our Lord we are returning." And when you alight from the ships and the livestock, say: "O Allah, cause us to alight in a blessed place, and You are the best of those who cause to alight." Ibn Abi Najih reported from Mujahid who said: whoever rides and does not say: "Exalted is He who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it under control," the devil says to him: "Sing," and if he does not do well, the devil says to him: "Wish." Al-Nahhas mentioned this. He seeks refuge in Allah from the state of one who says to his companions: "Come, let us take a pleasure ride on horses or in some boats," and they ride carrying with themselves vessels of wine and musical instruments, and they continue drinking until their tila' [Al-tila': what is boiled from grape juice until two-thirds of it is gone. Some Arabs call wine "tila'," intending by that to make its name seem pleasant.] is exhausted, while they are on the backs of beasts or in the hulls of ships that carry them, mentioning none but the devil and obeying none but his commands. Al-Zamakhshari said: It has reached me that some rulers rode while drinking wine from one city to another, the distance between them being a month's journey, and he did not become sober until the place had settled around him, so he was unaware of his journey and did not perceive it. How great is the difference between the deeds of those riders and what Allah has commanded in this verse!?

The she-camel razamat, yarzumu and yarzimu, razum and ruzam, when she stands from exhaustion and weakness and does not move, so she is razim. Said by al-Jawhari in al-Sihah."], and he said: "As for me, indeed I am able to control this one." He said: so she kicked him, and his neck was broken. It is also reported that a Bedouin rode his young camel and said: "Indeed I am able to control it," so the young camel kicked him until she threw him down, and his neck was broken. Al-Mawardi mentioned the first and Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned the second. He said: a servant should not abandon saying this, though it is not obligatory to mention it by tongue. So he says whenever he rides, especially when traveling, if he remembers: "Exalted is He who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it under control. And indeed to our Lord we are returning." O Allah, You are the companion on the journey and the successor over the family and property. O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the hardship of travel, the sorrow of returning, the injustice after the union, and the evil sight regarding family and property. By "the injustice after the union" he means the scattering of a man's affairs after they were gathered. 'Amr ibn Dinar said: I rode with Abu Ja'far to a land of his, near a garden called Mudrika, and he mounted a difficult camel. I said to him: "Abu Ja'far! Are you not afraid it will throw you?" He said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "On the hump of every camel is a devil; when you ride them, mention the name of Allah as He commanded you, then make them serve you, for Allah carries them." 'Ali ibn Rabi'a said: I witnessed 'Ali ibn Abi Talib ride a beast one day. When he placed his foot in the stirrup, he said: "In the name of Allah." When he settled on the beast, he said: "Praise be to Allah." Then he said: "Exalted is He who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it under control. And indeed to our Lord we are returning." Then he said: "Praise be to Allah, and Allah is greatest" three times, "O Allah, there is no god but You; I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You." Then he laughed. I said to him: "What made you laugh?" He said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ do as I did, and say as I said, then he laughed. I said: 'What makes you laugh, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'The servant, or he said: wonder at a servant who says: O Allah, there is no god but You; I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You, knowing that no one else forgives sins.'" Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi recorded it in his Musnad, and Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Khuwaiz Mandad in his Ahkam. Al-Tha'labi mentioned something similar in summary from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and his wording from him is: that the Prophet ﷺ, when he placed his foot in the stirrup, said: "In the name of Allah." When he settled, he said: "Praise be to Allah for every state. Exalted is He who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it under control, and indeed to our Lord we are returning." And when you alight from the ships and the livestock, say: "O Allah, cause us to alight in a blessed place, and You are the best of those who cause to alight." Ibn Abi Najih reported from Mujahid who said: whoever rides and does not say: "Exalted is He who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it under control," the devil says to him: "Sing," and if he does not do well, the devil says to him: "Wish." Al-Nahhas mentioned this. He seeks refuge in Allah from the state of one who says to his companions: "Come, let us take a pleasure ride on horses or in some boats," and they ride carrying with themselves vessels of wine and musical instruments, and they continue drinking until their tila' [Al-tila': what is boiled from grape juice until two-thirds of it is gone. Some Arabs call wine "tila'," intending by that to make its name seem pleasant.] is exhausted, while they are on the backs of beasts or in the hulls of ships that carry them, mentioning none but the devil and obeying none but his commands. Al-Zamakhshari said: It has reached me that some rulers rode while drinking wine from one city to another, the distance between them being a month's journey, and he did not become sober until the place had settled around him, so he was unaware of his journey and did not perceive it. How great is the difference between the deeds of those riders and what Allah has commanded in this verse!?

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 15:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a portion﴾, meaning an equal (ʿidl), according to Qatada. He means whatever is worshipped besides Allah, mighty and majestic. Al-Zajjaj and al-Mubarrad said: the "juz'" (portion) here means daughters. The believers were astonished at their ignorance, since they acknowledged that the Creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah, and then they made for Him a partner [[In L: partners.]] or a son, and they did not realize that whoever is able to create the heavens and the earth has no need of anything to support him or to be company for him, because that is among the attributes of deficiency. Al-Mawardi said: According to the scholars of Arabic, the "juz'" is daughters. It is said: "The woman has given birth to daughters (ajza'at al-mar'ah)" when she bears daughters. The poet said:

If a free woman bears daughters one day, there is no wonder, for a free woman may sometimes bear only males (al-midhkar) at other times.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Among the innovations in exegesis is the interpretation of "juz'" as females, and the claim that "juz'" in the Arabic language is a name for females. This is nothing but a lie against the Arabs and a newly invented, altered coinage. It did not satisfy them until they derived from it: "ajza'at al-mar'ah," and then made a verse, saying:

If a free woman bears daughters one day, there is no wonder; I have married her to a daughter of al-Aws, one who bears daughters.

[[Its completion, as in Lisan, root j-z-'': "For the pliant spear-shaft among her tents is a rustling."]]

Rather, His saying, "And they have made for Him from His servants a portion," is connected to His saying, "And if you asked them," that is, if you asked them about the Creator of the heavens and the earth, they would certainly acknowledge Him; yet, along with that acknowledgment, they have made for Him a portion from His servants, and attributed to Him the attributes of created beings. The meaning of "a portion from His servants" is that they said the angels are the daughters of Allah, so they made them a part of Him and a piece of Him, just as a child is a part of his father and a portion of him. It is also read "juzuʾ" with two dammas. ﴿Indeed, man﴾, meaning the disbeliever, ﴿is clearly ungrateful﴾. Al-Hasan said: He counts the calamities and forgets the blessings. "Mubin" means one who manifests disbelief.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 16:

Allah's words: ﴿Has He taken daughters from what He creates, and chosen sons for you?﴾ The mim (al-mim) is a connecting particle (silah), its implied sense being: "Has He taken daughters from what He creates, as you claim that the angels are the daughters of Allah?" Its wording is that of a question, but its meaning is rebuke (tawbikh).

"And has chosen you with sons," i.e., He has singled you out and purified you for sons. It is said: "I chose him (asfaytuhu) with such-and-such," meaning I preferred him with it. "I gave him sincere affection (asfaytuhu al-wudd)," meaning I made it pure for him. "Safaytuhu" and "tasafaynaa" mean we were sincere to one another (takhalasna).

He marvels at their attributing to Allah the choice of daughters while they themselves choose sons for themselves, and He is exalted above having a child. If an ignorant person imagines that He has taken a child for Himself, why did He not attribute to Himself the nobler of the two kinds? Why did these people assign to themselves the nobler of the two kinds and to Him the lesser? This is like the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him? That, then, is an unjust division!﴾ [al-Najm: 21–22].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When one of them is given good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness﴾, i.e., that a daughter has been born to him, "his face becomes dark" (ẓalla wajhuhu), i.e., his face becomes "blackened" (musawwadan). It was said: this refers to the invalidity of the likeness he has coined. And it was said: it refers to what he was given good news of, namely the female. Its evidence is in Surah al-Nahl: ﴿When one of them is given good news of a female﴾ [al-Nahl: 58]. [[See vol. 10, p. 116.]] Part of their condition was that when one of them was told that a female had been born to him, he would become distressed, his face would darken with rage and grief, and he would be filled with anguish. It is reported of some Arabs that his wife gave birth to a girl, so he shunned the house in which the woman was, and she said:

What is with Abu Hamza that he does not come to us,
Staying in the room that is near us,
Angry that we do not bear sons?
We only take what we are given.

In another reading: "jamratu" with a jim. In Bulugh al-Arab by al-Alusi: "li-abi wal-dhalqa'".

And it is read "musawwadan" and "musawwad". According to the reading of the majority, "wajhuhu" is the subject of "ẓalla" and "musawwadan" is the predicate of "ẓalla". It is also permissible that "ẓalla" contains a pronoun referring to "one of them", which is its subject, with "wajhuhu" as an appositive to the pronoun, and "musawwadan" as the predicate of "ẓalla". It is also permissible that "wajhuhu" be in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), with "musawwadan" in the nominative as its predicate, and "ẓalla" with its subject forming the predicate of that clause.

﴿And he is kazim﴾, i.e., grieving. This is what Qatadah said. It was said: distressed, as 'Ikrimah said. It was said: silent, as Ibn Abi Hatim said. This is due to the corruption of his likeness and the invalidity of his argument.

Whoever permits that the angels are daughters of Allah has made the angels akin to Allah, because the offspring is of the same kind as the parent and resembles it. Whoever's face blackens over what is attributed to him that he does not approve of is more deserving than one whose face blackens by attributing such a thing to one who is greater than him, so how much more so to Allah, mighty and majestic!

What has passed in Surah al-Nahl regarding the meaning of this verse is sufficient. [[See vol. 10, p. 116.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 18–19:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is one who is brought up among ornaments...?﴾ In it there are two issues. The first: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Is one who is brought up...﴾, meaning he is reared and grows up. Nusho' (nushu') means upbringing. It is said: "I grew up (nasha'tu) among the family of so-and-so, a growing up (nusha'an and nushu'an) when I grew up among them." Nushshi'a and unshi'a have the same meaning. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Ibn Wathhab, Hafs, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read yunashsha'u with a damma on the yaa', a fatha on the nun and a shadda on the shin, meaning he is reared and raised up among ornaments. Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading, because the attribution (isnad) in it is higher. The rest read yansha'u with a fatha on the yaa' and a sukun on the nun, and Abu Hatim preferred this, meaning he is firmly established and grows. Its root is from nasha'a, meaning he rose up, as al-Harawi said. So "yunsha'" is transitive and "yan sha'" is intransitive. The second: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿among ornaments﴾, meaning in adornment. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: they are the women, whose dress is not the dress of men. Mujahid said: women were granted permission regarding gold and silk, and he recited this verse. Al-Kiya al-Harrasi said: in it there is evidence for the permissibility of jewelry for women, and consensus has been established upon it, and the reports concerning it are countless.

I (al-Qurtubi) say: It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he used to say to his daughter: "O my little daughter, beware of adorning yourself with gold! For I fear for you the flame (allahab)."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and he, in disputation, is not clear﴾, meaning in argument and in presenting proof. Qatadah said: no woman ever spoke while having a proof except that she turned it against herself. In the codex of Abdullah it reads "wa huwa fi al-khisam ghayru mubin." The meaning of the verse is: Is such a one attributed to Allah? That is, it is not permissible. It has also been said: the one brought up among ornaments is their idols, which they fashioned from gold and silver and adorned, as Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak said. And the meaning of "and he, in disputation, is not clear" according to this view is: he is silent with respect to the answer. "Man" is in the accusative position, meaning they assigned to Allah one who is brought up among ornaments. It is also permissible that it be nominative, as an inchoative with an implied predicate, as al-Farra' said, its estimated sense being: or one who is in this state deserves worship. If you wish, you may say it is genitive, referring back to the beginning of the speech, which is his saying "bi-ma darab" (what he struck as an example), or to "mimma" in his saying "mimma yakhluqu banat" (of what He creates daughters). The substitution (badal) in these two places is weak, because the interrogative alif intervenes between the substitute and the substituted.

﴿And they made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾. The Kufans read "'ibad" in the plural. Abu 'Ubayd preferred this, because the attribution in it is higher, and because Allah, Exalted is He, only denied their claim that they are the daughters of Allah; so He informed them that they are servants and not His daughters. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited "'ibad al-Rahman," and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "In my codex it is 'abd al-Rahman." He said: "Erase it and write 'ibad al-Rahman." Confirming this reading is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, they are honoured servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26]. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do those who disbelieve think that they may take My servants (ibadi) as protectors besides Me?﴾ [al-Kahf: 102]. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed those whom you invoke besides Allah are servants (ibad) like you﴾ [al-A'raf: 194]. The rest read "'inda al-Rahman" with a silent nun, and Abu Hatim preferred this. Confirming this reading is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed those who are with your Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 206], and His saying: ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and those who are with Him﴾ [al-Anbiya': 19]. The purpose is to clarify their lie and to show their ignorance in attributing offspring to Allah, Glorified is He, and then in their judgment that the angels are females while they are the daughters of Allah. Mentioning the servants is a praise of them, meaning: how could they worship one who is at the pinnacle of worship, and then how could they rule that they are females without any proof? The word "ja'ala" here carries the sense of saying and judging; you say: "I made Zayd the most knowledgeable of people," meaning I judged him to be so.

﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ meaning: were they present at the time of their creation, so that they judged them to be females? It has been said: the Prophet ﷺ asked them and said: ["What then makes you know that they are females?"] They said: "We heard that from our fathers, and we testify that they did not lie in saying that they are females." Then Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Their testimony will be recorded and they will be questioned﴾, meaning they will be questioned about it in the Hereafter.

Nafi' read "a-shahidu" (aa-shahidu) with an interrogative hamza entering upon a softened damma-hamza, and he does not elongate it except what al-Musayyabi narrated from him, that he elongated it. Al-Mufaddal narrated from 'Asim the same, with both hamzas realized. The rest read "ashahidu" with a single hamza for interrogation. It is narrated from al-Zuhri "ushhidu khalqahum" as a statement. "Satuktabu" is the reading of the common people with a damma on the ta' as a passive verb, "shahadatuhum" in the nominative. Al-Sulami, Ibn al-Sumayqa' and Hubayra from Hafs read "sanaktubu" with a nun, "shahadatuhum" in the accusative by making the verb active. From Abu Raja': "satuktabu shahadatuhum" in the plural.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾. That is, the polytheists said, mockingly and derisively: "If the Most Merciful had willed, according to your claim, we would not have worshipped these angels." And this, from them, is a word of truth by which falsehood is intended. Everything happens by the will of Allah, and His will is necessary, as is His knowledge; therefore it is not possible to argue by it, and it contradicts what is known. What is willed is within His power even if it does not occur. And if they had worshipped Allah instead of the idols, we would know that Allah willed from them what came about from them. This meaning has already passed in al-An'am at His saying: ﴿The idolaters will say, "If Allah had willed, we would not have associated anything with Him"﴾ [al-An'am: 148][[See vol. 7, p. 3 (128)]], and in Ya-Sin: ﴿Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 47][[See vol. 15, p. 37]].

His saying, "They have no knowledge of it" (ma lahum bidhalika min 'ilm), refers back to His saying: ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19]. That is, they have no knowledge, by their saying that the angels are daughters of Allah. This was said by Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Kalbi. Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: it means the idols, that is, they have no knowledge for worshipping the idols. "Min" (min) is an extra particle (silah). "They only guess" (in hum illa yakhrusun), that is, they conjecture and lie, so they have no excuse for worshipping other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic. And within their speech was the implication that Allah had commanded us to do this, or was pleased with it from us; and for this reason He did not forbid us and did not hasten punishment upon us.

This is a parallel to His saying, ﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ The meaning: Were they present at their creation, or have We given them a Book before it, i.e., before the Qur'an, supporting what they claim, so that they hold fast to it and act upon what is in it?

In this passage there are two issues.

The first is His saying, ﴿upon a community﴾, meaning upon a way and a creed. This was said by ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz. He, Mujahid and Qatadah used to read ﴿عَلَى إِمَّةٍ﴾ *ʿalā immatin*, with a kasra on the alif. *Al-immah* means the way. Al-Jawhari said: *al-immah* (with a kasra) means blessing. *Al-immah* is also a dialect form of *al-ummah*, which means the way and the religion, from Abu ʿUbaydah. ʿAdi ibn Zayd said, referring to blessing:

Then after success, kingship and blessing,
the graves sheltered them there.

This is from other than al-Jawhari. Qatadah and ʿAtiyyah said: ﴿upon a community﴾ means upon a religion. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

We were upon the community of our fathers,
and the latter follows the former.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-ummah* means the way and the religion. It is said: "So-and-so has no *ummah*," meaning he has no religion and no creed. The poet said:

Can one who has a creed be equal to one who disbelieves?

Mujahid and Qutrub said: upon a religion, upon a creed. In some codices it reads: "They said, indeed we found our fathers upon a creed." These statements are close in meaning. It is related from al-Farra' that *ʿalā millatin* means upon a direction of prayer. Al-Akhfash said: upon uprightness. He recited the saying of al-Nabighah:

I swore, and left you no doubt,
and would one who has a creed sin while he is obedient?

The second issue concerns His saying, ﴿Indeed we are upon their traces guided﴾, meaning we are guided by them. In the other verse it reads ﴿muqtadun﴾, meaning we follow them, and the meaning is the same. Qatadah said: *muqtadun* means followers. In this there is evidence for the invalidity of *taqlid* (blind imitation), since He censured them for imitating their fathers and abandoning reflection on what the Messenger ﷺ called them to. This matter has already been discussed in full in *al-Baqarah*. [[See vol. 2 p. 211 onward, second edition.]]

Muqatil related that this verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Sufyan, Abu Jahl, and ʿUtbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabiʿah, from Quraysh. That is, just as these people said, those before them also said. It consoles His Prophet ﷺ. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾ [Fussilat 43]. *Al-mutraf* means the one given luxury, and what is meant here is kings and tyrants.

In this passage there are two issues.

The first is His saying, ﴿upon a community﴾, meaning upon a way and a creed. This was said by ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz. He, Mujahid and Qatadah used to read ﴿عَلَى إِمَّةٍ﴾ *ʿalā immatin*, with a kasra on the alif. *Al-immah* means the way. Al-Jawhari said: *al-immah* (with a kasra) means blessing. *Al-immah* is also a dialect form of *al-ummah*, which means the way and the religion, from Abu ʿUbaydah. ʿAdi ibn Zayd said, referring to blessing:

Then after success, kingship and blessing,
the graves sheltered them there.

This is from other than al-Jawhari. Qatadah and ʿAtiyyah said: ﴿upon a community﴾ means upon a religion. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

We were upon the community of our fathers,
and the latter follows the former.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-ummah* means the way and the religion. It is said: "So-and-so has no *ummah*," meaning he has no religion and no creed. The poet said:

Can one who has a creed be equal to one who disbelieves?

Mujahid and Qutrub said: upon a religion, upon a creed. In some codices it reads: "They said, indeed we found our fathers upon a creed." These statements are close in meaning. It is related from al-Farra' that *ʿalā millatin* means upon a direction of prayer. Al-Akhfash said: upon uprightness. He recited the saying of al-Nabighah:

I swore, and left you no doubt,
and would one who has a creed sin while he is obedient?

The second issue concerns His saying, ﴿Indeed we are upon their traces guided﴾, meaning we are guided by them. In the other verse it reads ﴿muqtadun﴾, meaning we follow them, and the meaning is the same. Qatadah said: *muqtadun* means followers. In this there is evidence for the invalidity of *taqlid* (blind imitation), since He censured them for imitating their fathers and abandoning reflection on what the Messenger ﷺ called them to. This matter has already been discussed in full in *al-Baqarah*. [[See vol. 2 p. 211 onward, second edition.]]

Muqatil related that this verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Sufyan, Abu Jahl, and ʿUtbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabiʿah, from Quraysh. That is, just as these people said, those before them also said. It consoles His Prophet ﷺ. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾ [Fussilat 43]. *Al-mutraf* means the one given luxury, and what is meant here is kings and tyrants.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, "The Compendium of the Rulings of the Qur'an") on surah 43, verse 24:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Said he: "Even if I brought you better guidance than what you found your fathers following?"﴾ That is, say, O Muhammad, to your people: "Have I not come to you from God with better guidance?" He means "more rightly guided" (*arshad*). ﴿"Than what you found your fathers following." They said: "We reject what you have been sent with."﴾ That is, with everything the messengers were sent with. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but its wording is plural, because denying him is denying whoever else was sent. It has been read as *qul* ("say"), *qala* ("he said"), *ji'tukum* and *ji'nakum* ("I came to you" and "We came to you"). The meaning is: "Will you follow your fathers, even if I brought you a religion more rightly guided than the religion of your fathers?" They said: "We remain steadfast in the religion of our fathers. We will never depart from it, even if you bring us something more rightly guided."

The discussion of *taqlid* (blind imitation of authority) and its condemnation has already passed in *al-Baqarah* [[Verse 43 of Surat Fussilat.]], so there is no point in repeating it.

Al-Qurtubi, in *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, on surah 43, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾, by drought, by killing and by captivity. "So see how was the end of those who denied," the final outcome of those who denied the messengers.

The recitation (qira'ah, a variant reading of the Qur'an) of the majority is "[[what is between the two brackets is from the previous verse]]": ﴿He said, "Even if I brought you…"﴾. Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read "He said, 'Even if…'" as a report about the warner, that he said this statement to them. Abu Ja'far read "Say, 'Even if we brought you…'" with a nun and an alif, on the basis that the address is from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to all the messengers. [

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verses 26–27:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when﴾, that is, remind them when ﴿he said﴾. "Ibrahim said to his father and his people: Indeed, I am free (*bara'*) from what you worship." *Al-bara'* is used for one person or more, and it is not made dual, plural or feminine, because it is a *masdar* (verbal noun) placed in the position of a *na't* (qualifying adjective). One does not say *al-bara'an* or *al-bara'un*, because the meaning is *dhu al-bara'* (possessor of disavowal) and *dhu al-bara'* in the plural. Al-Jawhari said: "*Tabarra'tu min kadha* (I disavowed such-and-such), and *ana minhu bara'* and *khala'* from it. It is not made dual or plural, because it is originally a *masdar*, like *sami'a sama'an* (he heard hearing)." When you say *ana bari'un minhu* and *khali*, it becomes dual, plural and feminine. In the plural you say *nahnu minhu bura'u*, like *faqih* and *fuqaha'*; also *biraa'*, like *karim* and *kiram*; also *abra'*, like *sharif* and *ashraf*; also *abriya'*, like *nasib* and *ansiba'*; and *bari'un*. A woman is *bari'a*, two women are *bari'atan*, and women are *bari'at* and *baraya*. A man is *bari'* and *bura'*, like *ajib* and *ujab*. *Al-bara'* (with a fatha) is the first night of the month, and it was so named because the moon disengages (*tabarru'*) from the sun.

﴿Except the One who originated me﴾ is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*), because they worshipped God alongside their gods. Qatadah said: "They used to say God is our Lord, while also worshipping idols." It is also permissible that it be a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*), meaning: "But the One who originated me, He is the one who guides me." He said this out of confidence in God and to alert his people that guidance comes from his Lord.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verses 26–27:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when﴾, that is, remind them when ﴿he said﴾. "Ibrahim said to his father and his people: Indeed, I am free (*bara'*) from what you worship." *Al-bara'* is used for one person or more, and it is not made dual, plural or feminine, because it is a *masdar* (verbal noun) placed in the position of a *na't* (qualifying adjective). ﴿Except the One who originated me﴾ is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*), because they worshipped God alongside their gods. Qatadah said: "They used to say God is our Lord, while also worshipping idols." It is also permissible that it be a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*), meaning: "But the One who originated me, He is the one who guides me." He said this out of confidence in God and to alert his people that guidance comes from his Lord.

There are three issues here.

**The first issue: Allah's words, "And He made it a word that remains" (﴿وَجَعَلَها كَلِمَةً باقِيَةً﴾).** The pronoun in "made it" (*ja'alaha*) refers to His words, "except He who created me" (﴿إِلَّا الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي﴾). The subject of "made it" is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The meaning is that Allah made this word and statement remain among his posterity (*'aqib*), namely his offspring and their offspring. That is, they inherited disavowal of worshipping other than Allah, and some of them enjoined it upon others. The *'aqib* (posterity, descendants) is whoever comes after him.

Al-Suddi said: they are the family of Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn Abbas said: His saying "among his posterity" means among his successors.

There is an inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) in the sentence. The meaning is: "Surely He will guide me, so that they may return" (﴿لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْجِعُونَ﴾), and "He made it a word that remains among his posterity" means that he said this to them so that they might repent of worshipping other than Allah.

Mujahid and Qatada said: the word is "There is no god but Allah" (*La ilaha illa Allah*). Qatada said: there will always be among his descendants someone who worships Allah until the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Dahhak said: the word is that you should not worship anyone but Allah.

Ikrima said: it is Islam, based on Allah's saying, "He named you Muslims before" (﴿هُوَ سَمَّاكُمُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾) [al-Hajj: 78].

[Footnote: the end of Surah al-Hajj.]

Al-Qurazi said: the bequest of Abraham, with which he enjoined his sons, namely his saying, "O my sons, surely Allah has chosen the religion for you" (﴿يَا بَنِيَّ إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفى لَكُمُ الدِّينَ﴾) [al-Baqarah: 132], the verse mentioned in al-Baqarah [Footnote: verse 132], is the "word that remains" among his offspring and sons.

Ibn Zayd said: the word is his saying, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds" (﴿أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ الْعالَمِينَ﴾) [al-Baqarah: 131], and he recited, "He named you Muslims before."

It has also been said: the word is prophethood (*nubuwwa*). Ibn al-'Arabi said: prophethood has never ceased to remain among the descendants of Abraham. The monotheism (*tawhid*) belongs to them in origin, and others follow them in it.

**The second issue:** Ibn al-'Arabi said: Abraham's (peace be upon him) descent, linked to the ages, was granted through his two answered supplications. The first is in his saying, "I am making you an imam for the people." He said, "And from my descendants?" He said, "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers" (﴿إِنِّي جاعِلُكَ لِلنَّاسِ إِمامًا قالَ وَمِنْ ذُرِّيَّتِي قالَ لا يَنالُ عَهْدِي الظَّالِمِينَ﴾) [al-Baqarah: 124]. So Allah said: yes, except those among them who do wrong, for them there is no covenant.

The second is His saying, "And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols" (﴿وَاجْنُبْنِي وَبَنِيَّ أَنْ نَعْبُدَ الْأَصْنامَ﴾) [Ibrahim: 35].

It has been said: rather, the first is his saying, "And make for me a tongue of truth among the later generations" (﴿وَاجْعَلْ لِي لِسانَ صِدْقٍ فِي الْآخِرِينَ﴾) [al-Shu'ara': 84], so every nation honors him, his sons and others who are united with him through Sam or Noah.

[Footnote: verse 124 of Surah al-Baqarah.] [Footnote: verse 35 of Surah Ibrahim.] [Footnote: verse 84 of Surah al-Shu'ara'.]

**The third issue:** Ibn al-'Arabi said: the mention of *'aqib* here is connected in meaning, and this belongs to the rulings on which the contracts of *'umra* (a grant of the use of property for the grantee's lifetime) and *tahbis* (endowment, *habs*) are based.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whichever man grants a *'umra* to someone and to his *'aqib*, it belongs to the one to whom it was given, and does not return to the one who gave it, because he gave a gift into which inheritance has entered." [Footnote: the *'umra* (as in *hubla*) is the transfer of ownership of a thing for the duration of a lifetime.]

It is applied to eleven terms.

*The first term:* *al-walad* (child). When used without qualification, it refers to whoever is born of a man and his wife, whether female or male. In language and in law, it refers to the offspring of males only, not of females. For this reason inheritance falls on the specified child and on the sons of the specified male children, not on the children of females, because they belong to other people. For this reason they are not included in an endowment by this term. Malik said this in *al-Majmu'a* and elsewhere.

I say: this is the position of Malik and all of his earlier companions. Among their proofs for this is the consensus (*ijma'*) that the children of daughters have no inheritance, along with His saying, "Allah instructs you concerning your children" (﴿يُوصِيكُمُ اللَّهُ فِي أَوْلادِكُمْ﴾) [al-Nisa': 11].

A group of scholars held that the children of daughters are among the children and descendants, and they enter endowments. The donor says: "I have endowed it for my child or for my posterity." This is the choice of Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr and others. They argued with Allah's saying, "Forbidden to you are your mothers and your daughters" (﴿حُرِّمَتْ عَلَيْكُمْ أُمَّهاتُكُمْ وَبَناتُكُمْ﴾) [al-Nisa': 23]. They said: since Allah forbade daughters, the daughter of a daughter is thereby forbidden by consensus, so it is known that she is a daughter, and she must enter her father's endowment if he endowed it for his child or posterity.

This meaning was discussed fully in al-An'am [Footnote: see vol. 7, p. 31].

*The second term:* *al-banun* (sons). If he says: "This is an endowment for my son," it does not extend beyond the specified child and does not multiply. If he says, "for my child (*walad*)," it extends and multiplies to everyone who is born. If he says, "for my sons (*banun*)," males and females enter it.

Malik said: whoever gives in charity to his sons and his sons' sons, his daughters and his daughters' daughters enter into that. 'Isa narrated from Ibn al-Qasim concerning one who endowed to his daughters that the daughters of his daughter enter with the daughters of his direct line. But the position of most of his companions is that the children of daughters do not enter into *al-banin*.

If it is said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said about al-Hasan, son of his daughter: "Surely this son of mine is a master, and perhaps Allah will reconcile through him between two great groups of Muslims." We say: this is figurative (*majaz*), and he referred to it to honor him and to give him precedence. Do you not see that it is permissible to negate it of him? A man may say about the child of his daughter, "He is not my son." If it were literal (*haqiqa*), its negation would not be permitted, because literal realities are not negated of what they belong to. Do you not see that a child is ascribed to his father and not to his mother? For this reason it was said of 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas that he is Hashimi and not Hilali, even though his mother was Hilali.

I say: this argument is not sound. Rather, the child of a daughter is a child in the literal sense in language, because the meaning of birth is present in him. And the scholars have agreed on the prohibition of a daughter's daughter, from the words of Allah, "Forbidden to you are your mothers and your daughters" (﴿حُرِّمَتْ عَلَيْكُمْ أُمَّهاتُكُمْ وَبَناتُكُمْ﴾) [al-Nisa': 23]. And He said, "And among his descendants, Dawud and Sulayman ... to ... the righteous" (﴿وَمِنْ ذُرِّيَّتِهِ داوُدَ وَسُلَيْمانَ ... مِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ﴾) [al-An'am: 84–85], so He made Isa among his descendants, although he was the son of his daughter, as explained earlier in that place.

If it is said: the poet said:
*Our sons are the sons of our sons, and our daughters' sons are the sons of distant men.*

It is said to them: there is no proof in this, because the meaning of his saying is only that the sons of his sons, males, are those who have the ruling of his sons in inheritance and lineage. The children of his daughters do not have the ruling of his daughters in this respect, since they are attributed to another. So he informed that they differ in ruling while agreeing in naming. He did not negate the name "child" from the children of daughters, since he is a son. A man may say of his child, "He is not my son," since he does not obey him and does not recognize his right. He does not mean by this to negate the name of child from him, but only to negate his ruling.

Whoever uses this verse as proof that a daughter's child is not called a child has corrupted its meaning and voided its benefit, and has interpreted the speaker in a way that is not valid. It is not possible in the Arabic language for a son's child not to be called a son while a daughter's child is not called a son, because the meaning of birth from which the name "child" is derived is clearer and stronger in him. The child of a daughter is her child in the true sense of birth, while the child of a son is his child only by his property and by what was the cause of birth.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, did not exclude the children of daughters from an endowment on "his child," because the name "child" does not apply to them in his understanding of the language. He excluded them only by analogy to inheritance. This was discussed earlier in al-An'am [Footnote: see vol. 7, p. 31], and praise belongs to Allah.

*The third term:* *al-dhurriyya* (offspring). It is derived from *dhara'a Allah al-khalq* (Allah created creation). It therefore includes the children of daughters, based on His saying, "And among his descendants, Dawud and Sulayman ... and Zakariyya and Yahya and Isa" (﴿وَمِنْ ذُرِّيَّتِهِ داوُدَ وَسُلَيْمانَ ... وَزَكَرِيَّا وَيَحْيى وَعِيسى﴾) [al-An'am: 84–85]. He was among his descendants only through his mother. The derivation of *dhurriyya* has already been discussed in al-Baqara [Footnote: see vol. 2, p. 107, second edition], and in al-An'am the discussion of "And among his descendants" (﴿وَمِنْ ذُرِّيَّتِهِ﴾) [al-An'am: 84] has been given, so there is no point in repeating it.

The Tenth Term: al-Qawm (the people). This is taken to mean the men of the clan (al-'asabah) only, to the exclusion of the women. Al-qawm may also include both men and women. The poet said:

*"I do not know, and I suppose I will come to know, whether the people of Hisn are men or women."*

But he meant that when a man calls his people for support, he means the men, and when he calls them for their sanctity (al-hurmah), both men and women are included. The context generalizes the term and the indicator restricts it.

The Eleventh Term: al-Mawali (clients or freedmen). Malik said: it includes the clients of his father and of his son together with his own clients. Ibn Wahb said: it includes the children of his clients. Ibn al-'Arabi said: what results from this is that it includes whoever inherits from him through wala' (the bond of patronage). He said: these are the detailed points of the discussion and its foundations, linked to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and to the Sunnah that clarifies it. Its branches and completions are in the book of questions. And God knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, but I gave enjoyment﴾. It is also read "Nay, but We gave enjoyment" (*balla matta'na*). ﴿To these and their fathers﴾, that is, in this world, through being granted respite. ﴿Until there came to them the Truth﴾, that is, Muhammad (ﷺ), with monotheism and Islam, which is the root of the religion of Ibrahim (Abraham), and it is the word that God left as a lasting principle among his descendants. ﴿And a clear Messenger﴾, that is, one who makes clear to them what they need to know.

﴿But when the Truth came to them﴾, meaning the Qur'an. ﴿They said, "This is sorcery, and we are disbelievers in it,"﴾ that is, deniers. ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down﴾, that is, "Why did it not come down ﴿upon a man﴾" — it is also read "upon a rajul" with the *jim* silent (*sukun*) — ﴿of the two cities, a great man?﴾ That is, from one of the two cities, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿From them both come forth pearls and coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], meaning from one of them. Or it means "upon one of two men from the two cities." The two cities are Makkah and al-Ta'if. The two men are al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn Makhzum, the paternal uncle of Abu Jahl, and the one from al-Ta'if is Abu Mas'ud Urwah ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi, as said by Qatadah. It is also said: Umayr ibn Abd Yalayl al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if, and Utbah ibn Rabi'ah from Makkah; this is the view of Mujahid. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that the great man of al-Ta'if was Habib ibn Amr al-Thaqafi. Al-Suddi said: Kinanah ibn Abd ibn Amr.

It is narrated that al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, who was called the "basil of Quraysh," used to say: "If what Muhammad says were true, it would have been sent down to me or to Abu Mas'ud." So God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾, meaning prophethood, so that they might place it wherever they wish. ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾, that is, We made some poor and some rich. Since the affairs of this world are not in their hands, how could the affairs of prophethood be entrusted to them?

Qatadah said: "One of them meets a man weak in strength, little in resource, and halting in speech, while he himself is given abundance, and he meets a man strong in resource, eloquent in speech, while he himself is kept in restriction" (*muqtar* in the text of *Ḥ Z L*, with the *fa*). Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Muhaysin, in one narration from him, read "*ma'ayishahum*" (their livelihoods). It is also said: that is, We gave the great man of the two cities what We gave, not because of their honour before Us, and I am able to withdraw blessing from them both; so what virtue or worth do they have?

﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees﴾, that is, We made some of them superior to others, so some are superior and some inferior, some leaders and some led, as said by Muqatil. It is also said: by freedom and slavery, so some are owners and some are owned. It is also said: by wealth and poverty, so some are rich and some are poor. It is also said: by commanding right and forbidding wrong.

﴿That some of them may take others in service (*sukhriyyan*)﴾. Al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: servants and attendants, so that the wealthy make the poor serve them, and thus some become the means of livelihood for others. Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: that is, that some may possess others. It is also said: it is from *al-sukhriyyah*, which means mockery, that is, that the rich may mock the poor. Al-Akhfash said: "I mocked him (*sakhirtu bihi*) and I mocked at him (*sakhirtu minhu*), I laughed at him and I laughed with him, I scoffed at him and I scoffed with him; both are said, and the noun is *al-sukhriyyah* (with a *damma*)." And *al-sukhriyy* and *al-sikhriyy* (with *damma* or *kasra*). All the readers read "*sukhriyyan*" with a *damma*, except Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid, who read "*sikhriyyan*" with a *kasra*.

﴿And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾, that is, more excellent than what they gather of the world. Then it is said: the mercy is prophethood. It is also said: Paradise. It is also said: completing the obligatory duties is better than the abundance of voluntary acts. It is also said: what is bestowed upon them by way of grace is better than what He rewards them for their deeds.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, but I gave enjoyment﴾. It is also read "Nay, but We gave enjoyment" (*balla matta'na*). ﴿To these and their fathers﴾, that is, in this world, through being granted respite. ﴿Until there came to them the Truth﴾, that is, Muhammad (ﷺ), with monotheism and Islam, which is the root of the religion of Ibrahim (Abraham), and it is the word that God left as a lasting principle among his descendants. ﴿And a clear Messenger﴾, that is, one who makes clear to them what they need to know.

﴿But when the Truth came to them﴾, meaning the Qur'an. ﴿They said, "This is sorcery, and we are disbelievers in it,"﴾ that is, deniers. ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down﴾, that is, "Why did it not come down ﴿upon a man﴾" — it is also read "upon a rajul" with the *jim* silent (*sukun*) — ﴿of the two cities, a great man?﴾ That is, from one of the two cities, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿From them both come forth pearls and coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], meaning from one of them. Or it means "upon one of two men from the two cities." The two cities are Makkah and al-Ta'if.
