**Fifth issue (the first):** The scholars said: [This verse] mentions the lowliness of this world and how little it is worth, and that it is so insignificant to Him that He would have made the houses and staircases of the disbelievers of gold and silver, were it not that love of this world dominates hearts, which would lead them to disbelief. Al-Hasan said: The meaning is: Were it not that all people would disbelieve because of their inclination toward this world and their neglect of the Hereafter, We would have given them in this world what We have described, because this world is worthless in the sight of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Most of the exegetes, including Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and others, held this view. Ibn Zayd said: ﴿Were it not that mankind would be one community﴾ in pursuit of this world and preferring it over the Hereafter, ﴿We would have given to those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: The meaning is: Were it not that among the disbelievers there would be rich and poor, and among the Muslims likewise, We would have given the disbelievers this much of the world, because of its worthlessness.

**Second issue:** Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "saqfan" (سَقْفًا) with a fatha on the sin and sukun on the qaf, in the singular, and its meaning is plural, by analogy with His words ﴿the roof fell on them from above them﴾ [al-Nahl: 26]. [See vol. 10, p. 97.] The rest read it with a damma on the sin and the qaf, in the plural, like "rahn" and "rihn" [pl. of pledge]. Abu 'Ubayd said: There is no third reading for them. It was also said that it is the plural of "saqif", like "kathib" and "kuthub", and "raghif" and "rughuf", as al-Farra' said. It was also said that it is the plural of "suqif", so it becomes a plural of a plural: "saqf" and "suqif", like "fals" and "fulus". Then they treated "fu'ul" as if it were a single noun and pluralised it as "fu'ul". It is also narrated from Mujahid that he read "saqfan" with a sukun on the qaf. It was also said that the lam in "li-buyutihim" means "'ala" (on), i.e., on their houses. It was also said that it is a substitution (badal), as you say: "I did this for Zayd for his honour", and Allah said: ﴿and for his parents, to each of them is a sixth﴾ [al-Nisa': 11]. [See vol. 5, p. 54.] Likewise He says here: ﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, for their houses...﴾.

**Third issue:** His words ﴿and staircases﴾ mean stairways, said Ibn 'Abbas, and this is the view of the majority. Its singular is "mi'raj", and "al-mi'raj" is a ladder, from which comes "laylat al-mi'raj" (the Night of the Ascent). The plural is "ma'arij" and "ma'arij", like "mafatih" and "mafatih" [keys]; both are dialectal forms. Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi and Talhah ibn Musarrif read "ma'arib", and these are the steps and staircases. Al-Akhfash said: If you wish, you may make the singular "mi'raj" or "ma'raj", like "mirqat" and "marqat" [step]. ﴿On which they ascend﴾: that is, they climb and rise upon the staircases; one says "zahartu 'ala al-bayt" (I ascended the roof of the house), meaning I went up onto its roof. This is because whoever ascends something and rises above it becomes visible to onlookers. It is also said: "zahartu 'ala al-shay'" means I knew it, and "zahartu 'ala al-'aduww" means I overcame the enemy. Nabigha of Banu Ja'dah recited to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ his line:

*"We ascended the sky in glory and awe, and we hope for a higher place than that."* [There are variant versions of this line: as in *Kitab al-Aghani*, vol. 5, p. 8, Dar al-Kutub al-Misriyyah edition:

"Our glory and our forebears have reached the sky."

As in *Jamharat Ash'ar al-'Arab*:

"Our glory, our munificence and our lordship have reached the sky."

As in *Lisan al-'Arab*, under the root "z-h-r":

"Our glory and our splendour have reached the sky."]

He meant "mis'adan" (a place of ascent), and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ became angry and said: "Where to?" He said: "To Paradise." He said: "Indeed, if Allah wills." Al-Hasan said: By Allah, this world has inclined toward most of its people, and yet He did not do it! So how would it be if He had done it?!

**Fourth issue:** Some scholars used this verse as evidence that the roof (saqf) has no right attached to the owner of the upper storey, because Allah made roofs for houses just as He made doors for them. This is the position of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is because "the house" (al-bayt) is a designation for a floor, a wall, a roof and a door, so whoever owns the house owns its components. There is no disagreement that the upper storey belongs to its owner up to the sky. They differed regarding the lower storey: some said it belongs to him, and some said he has no right to anything below the surface of the earth. Both opinions exist in our school. The authentic hadith of the Israelite man, mentioned earlier, has clarified this: a man sold a house to another man, who built on it and found in it a jar of gold. He brought it to the seller and said: "I bought the house, not the jar." The seller said: "I sold the house with what is in it." Each of them pushed it back to the other, so the Prophet ﷺ ruled between them that one of them should marry his son to the other's daughter, and the wealth would belong to both of them. The sound position is that the upper and lower storeys belong to the owner, unless he sells them out of his possession. If one of them sells one of the two parts, he retains from it what he benefits from, and the rest belongs to the buyer.

**Fifth issue:** Among the rulings on the upper and lower storeys: when the upper and lower storeys belong to two men, and the lower storey falls into disrepair, or its owner wants to demolish it, Sahnun reported from Ashhab that he said: If the owner of the lower storey wants to demolish it, or the owner of the upper storey wants to build upon his storey, the owner of the lower storey may not demolish it except out of necessity, and his demolition is more considerate to the owner of the upper storey, so that the upper storey does not collapse with the collapse of the lower one. The owner of the upper storey may not build on his storey anything that did not exist before, except a light thing that does not harm the owner of the lower storey. If a beam in the roof of the upper storey breaks, he may put a beam in its place that is no heavier than it, if its harm to the owner of the lower storey is feared. Ashhab said: The door of the house belongs to the owner of the lower storey. He said: If the lower storey collapses, its owner is compelled to rebuild it, and the owner of the upper storey is not obliged to build the lower storey. If the owner of the lower storey refuses to build, he is told: Sell it to someone who will build. Ibn al-Qasim narrated from Malik concerning a lower storey belonging to one man and an upper storey belonging to another, when the lower storey falls into disrepair: its repair is the responsibility of the owner of the lower storey, and he must keep the upper storey suspended until his lower storey is repaired, because he must either support it with a building or with a suspension. Likewise, if there is a storey above the upper storey, the suspension of the second upper storey is the responsibility of the owner of the middle storey. It has also been said that the suspension of the second upper storey is the responsibility of the owner of the upper storey, until he builds the lower one.

The hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The likeness of one who upholds the limits of Allah and one who violates them is like a people who drew lots for a ship: some of them got its upper part and some its lower part. Those in its lower part, when they needed water, would pass by those above them, and they said: 'If we made a hole in our share, we would not harm those above us.' If the others leave them to what they want, they will all perish together; and if they take hold of their hands, they will be saved and all will be saved together." [This is a foundational principle in this matter. It is evidence for Malik and Ashhab. It indicates that the owner of the lower storey may not cause harm to the owner of the upper storey, and that if he causes harm to him, he is obliged to repair it, not the owner of the upper storey; and that the owner of the upper storey has the right to prevent him from causing harm. Seizing the hand is only permitted against the wrongdoer, or against one who is prohibited from doing what is not lawful for him according to the Sunnah. It also indicates that one deserves punishment for abandoning enjoining good and forbidding evil, which has been discussed in "al-Anfal" [vol. 7, p. 391 onward]. It also indicates the permissibility of casting lots and using them, which was discussed in "Al 'Imran".]

So reflect on each matter in its place, and you will find it explained. And praise be to Allah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 34–35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for their houses, doors⦆ means: and We would have made for their houses. It is also said that "for their houses" is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for His saying "for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful." "Doors" means of silver. "And couches" likewise, and it is the plural of sarir (couch). It is also said it is the plural of al-asirrah, and al-asirrah is the plural of sarir, so it is a plural of a plural. ﴿Upon which they recline⦆: al-ittika' and al-tawakku' mean leaning heavily on a thing, and from it comes "atawakka'u ʿalayha" (I lean upon it). A man who is a tuka'ah, on the pattern of humazah, is one who leans much. Al-tuka'ah also means that upon which one leans. And "ittaka'a ʿala al-shay'" means he leaned on the thing, so he is muttaki'; the place is mutaka'. "Wa taʿanahu hatta atkaʾahu" (he struck him until he made him lean) on the pattern of af'alahu, meaning he cast him in the posture of one reclining. And "tawakkaʾtu ʿala al-ʿasa" (I leaned on the staff). The original of the ta' in all of this is a waw, so it was treated as was done with ittazana and ittaʿada.

﴿And adornment (zukhruf)⦆: here zukhruf means gold, according to Ibn ʿAbbas and others. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿or you have a house of zukhruf⦆ [al-Isra': 93], and it has already been mentioned [see vol. 10, p. 331]. Ibn Zayd said: it is what people acquire for their homes of goods and furnishings. Al-Hasan said: decorations (al-nuqush), and its origin is adornment. It is said: "zakhrafta al-dar," meaning I adorned the house, and "tazakhrafa fulan," meaning he adorned himself. "Zukhrufan" is in the accusative, in the sense of "and We made for them, along with that, zukhrufan." It is also said that the preposition is omitted, and the meaning is: So We made for them roofs, doors, and couches of silver and of gold; then, since "min" was omitted, He said "zukhrufan" and put it in the accusative.

﴿And all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the life of this world⦆: ʿAsim, Hamzah, and Hisham on the authority of Ibn ʿAmir read "wa-in kullu dhalika lamma mataʿu al-hayat al-dunya" with tashdid (intensive). The rest read it with takhfif (lightening). This has already been mentioned. It is narrated from Abu Raja' that he read the lam of "lamma" with a kasrah, so "ma" in his reading has the function of "alladhi," and the returning pronoun to it is omitted. The estimate is: "wa-in kullu dhalika lilladhi huwa mataʿu al-hayat al-dunya," and the omission of the pronoun here is like its omission in the reading of the one who read ﴿mathalan ma baʿudatan fama fawqaha⦆ [al-Baqarah: 26], and ﴿tamaman ʿala alladhi ahsan⦆ [al-An'am: 154]. Abu al-Fath said: in this reading "kull" should be in the accusative, because "in" is the lightened form of the heavy one (inna), and when it is lightened and its action is nullified, the lam must follow in the end of the sentence to distinguish it from the negating "in" which means "ma," as in: "in zaydun la-qa'im." There is no lam here other than the prepositional lam.

﴿And the Hereafter with your Lord is for the God-fearing⦆: it means Paradise for whoever fears God and is wary. Ka'b said: I find in some of the revealed books of God: "Were it not that My believing servant would grieve, I would crown the head of My disbelieving servant with a diadem, and his head would not split, nor would a vein throb in him with pain." It is in the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever." And from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If the world were worth in God's sight the wing of a gnat, He would not have given a disbeliever a drink of water from it." On this subject there is also a report from Abu Hurayrah; and he (al-Tirmidhi) said: it is a hasan gharib hadith.

And they recited:

If the world were a reward for the virtuous, then there would be no livelihood in it for the wrongdoer.
Prophets hungered in it out of honor, while the bellies of beasts were sated in it.

And another said:

Enjoy the days if you are prudent, for you are in them between one who forbids and one who commands.
If the world leaves a man his religion, then what he lost of it does not harm him.
So the world does not weigh the wing of a gnat, nor the weight of a feather's shred from a bird's wing.
He did not accept the world as a reward for the virtuous, nor did he accept the world as a punishment for the disbeliever.

It is also said it is the plural of al-asirrah, and al-asirrah is the plural of sarir, so it is a plural of a plural. ﴿Upon which they recline⦆: al-ittika' and al-tawakku' mean leaning heavily on a thing, and from it comes "atawakka'u ʿalayha" (I lean upon it). A man who is a tuka'ah, on the pattern of humazah, is one who leans much. Al-tuka'ah also means that upon which one leans. And "ittaka'a ʿala al-shay'" means he leaned on the thing, so he is muttaki'; the place is mutaka'. "Wa taʿanahu hatta atkaʾahu" (he struck him until he made him lean) on the pattern of af'alahu, meaning he cast him in the posture of one reclining. And "tawakkaʾtu ʿala al-ʿasa" (I leaned on the staff). The original of the ta' in all of this is a waw, so it was treated as was done with ittazana and ittaʿada.

﴿And adornment (zukhruf)⦆: here zukhruf means gold, according to Ibn ʿAbbas and others. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿or you have a house of zukhruf⦆ [al-Isra': 93], and it has already been mentioned [see vol. 10, p. 331]. Ibn Zayd said: it is what people acquire for their homes of goods and furnishings. Al-Hasan said: decorations (al-nuqush), and its origin is adornment. It is said: "zakhrafta al-dar," meaning I adorned the house, and "tazakhrafa fulan," meaning he adorned himself. "Zukhrufan" is in the accusative, in the sense of "and We made for them, along with that, zukhrufan." It is also said that the preposition is omitted, and the meaning is: So We made for them roofs, doors, and couches of silver and of gold; then, since "min" was omitted, He said "zukhrufan" and put it in the accusative.

﴿And all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the life of this world⦆: ʿAsim, Hamzah, and Hisham on the authority of Ibn ʿAmir read "wa-in kullu dhalika lamma mataʿu al-hayat al-dunya" with tashdid (intensive). The rest read it with takhfif (lightening). This has already been mentioned. It is narrated from Abu Raja' that he read the lam of "lamma" with a kasrah, so "ma" in his reading has the function of "alladhi," and the returning pronoun to it is omitted. The estimate is: "wa-in kullu dhalika lilladhi huwa mataʿu al-hayat al-dunya," and the omission of the pronoun here is like its omission in the reading of the one who read ﴿mathalan ma baʿudatan fama fawqaha⦆ [al-Baqarah: 26], and ﴿tamaman ʿala alladhi ahsan⦆ [al-An'am: 154]. Abu al-Fath said: in this reading "kull" should be in the accusative, because "in" is the lightened form of the heavy one (inna), and when it is lightened and its action is nullified, the lam must follow in the end of the sentence to distinguish it from the negating "in" which means "ma," as in: "in zaydun la-qa'im." ﴿And the Hereafter with your Lord is for the God-fearing⦆: it means Paradise for whoever fears God and is wary. Ka'b said: I find in some of the revealed books of God: "Were it not that My believing servant would grieve, I would crown the head of My disbelieving servant with a diadem, and his head would not split, nor would a vein throb in him with pain." It is in the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever." On this subject there is also a report from Abu Hurayrah; and he (al-Tirmidhi) said: it is a hasan gharib hadith.

And they recited:

If the world were a reward for the virtuous, then there would be no livelihood in it for the wrongdoer.
Prophets hungered in it out of honor, while the bellies of beasts were sated in it.

And another said:

Enjoy the days if you are prudent, for you are in them between one who forbids and one who commands.
If the world leaves a man his religion, then what he lost of it does not harm him.
So the world does not weigh the wing of a gnat, nor the weight of a feather's shred from a bird's wing.
He did not accept the world as a reward for the virtuous, nor did he accept the world as a punishment for the disbeliever.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 43, verses 36–38:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he becomes his constant companion﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah recited "wa-man ya'sha" (وَمَنْ يَعْشَ) with a fatha on the shin, meaning "becomes blind." It is said of this verb: "'ashiya ya'sha 'ashan" when one becomes blind. A man is called *a'sha* and a woman *'shawa'* when he or she cannot see. From this is the verse of al-A'sha:

*He saw a man whose two temples had vanished, / of misshapen form, blind and sightless.* [[In *al-Lisan*, under the root *w-f-d*: "The two *wafidan* in the poetry of al-A'sha are the two protrusions of the cheeks when chewing. When a person grows old, his two wafidan disappear."]]

And his saying:

*Did she see a man, a blind one, whom the vicissitudes of fate harmed, / and the age that is senile and enfeebled?*

The rest of the reciters read it with a damma (ya'su, يَعْشُو), from "'asa ya'su," when one suffers what the blind man suffers. Al-Khalil said: *al-'uswu* is looking with weak sight. He recited:

*Whenever you come to him, you squint toward the light of his fire, / you will find the best fire there, and the best kindler.* [[The verse is by al-Hutay'ah.]]

Another said:

*What a fine youth, who squints toward the light of his fire / when the wind blows and the place is barren.*

Al-Jawhari said: *al-'ashá* (with a short final alif) is the verbal noun of *a'sha*, who cannot see at night but can see by day. The feminine is *'shawa'*, and the dual feminine is *'shawawan*. "A'shahu Allah, fa-'shiya" (with kasra) means "God made him blind, so he became blind," in the form *ya'shá 'ashan*. The two (masculine) are *ya'shayan*, and they did not say *ya'shuwan*, because the waw, when it became a ya because of the kasra before it, was kept as it is in the dual. *Ta'ashá* means he showed himself as one who is blind. The relative form of *a'sha* is *a'shawiyy*, and of *al-'ashiyyah* (evening) is *'ashawiyy*. *Al-'shawa'* is the she-camel that cannot see in front of her, so she gropes with her hands at everything. "Fulan rakiba al-'shawa'" means he acted without insight, and "Fulan khabit khabt 'shawa'" means he is one who acts blindly.

This verse connects to the opening of the surah: ﴿Shall We then withhold the Reminder from you and turn away from you?﴾ [[verse 5]] [al-Zukhruf: 5], meaning: shall We not continue to send the Reminder to you? So whoever turns away from that Reminder, by averting from it toward the words and falsehoods of those who lead astray, "We appoint for him a devil," meaning We cause a devil to be assigned to him as recompense for his disbelief. "Then he becomes his constant companion." It was said that this refers to the world: he prevents him from what is lawful, drives him toward what is unlawful, forbids him obedience, and commands him to sin. This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

It was also said that it refers to the Hereafter, when he rises from his grave. This was said by Sa'id al-Jurayri. In a report: when the disbeliever comes out of his grave, he is accompanied by a devil who does not leave him until both enter the Fire. And the believer is accompanied by an angel until God judges among His creatures. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi. Al-Qushayri said: the correct view is that "he becomes his constant companion" applies in both the world and the Hereafter.

Abu al-Haytham and al-Azhari said: "'shawtu ila kadha" means I aimed at it, and "'shawtu 'an kadha" means I turned away from it, so they distinguish between *ila* and *'an*, as in "miltu ilayhi" and "miltu 'anhu." Qatadah likewise said: *ya'shu* means "turns away," and this is the view of al-Farra'. Al-Nahhas said: this is not known in the language. Al-Qurazi said: "he turns his back," and the meaning is the same. Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: "his eye becomes dark." Al-'Utbi denied that *'shawtu* means *a'radtu* (I turned away), and said: the correct form is *ta'ashaytu*. The view of Abu al-Haytham and al-Azhari is the correct one, and all people of knowledge agree with it.

Al-Sulami, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ya'qub, 'Ismah from 'Asim, and al-A'mash recited "yuqayyid" (يُقَيِّضُ) with ya' (yuqayyidu), because "al-Rahman" was mentioned first, meaning: the Most Merciful appoints for him a devil. The rest read it with nun (nuqayyid). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "yuqayyadu lahu shaytanun, fa-huwa lahu qarin," meaning "a constant companion" (*mulazim* and *musahib*).

It was said: "fa-huwa" refers to the devil, as already mentioned. It was also said: it refers to the turning away from the Qur'an, meaning he is a companion of the devil.

"And indeed they bar them from the way," meaning the devils bar them from the way of guidance. The plural is used because "man" in "wa-man ya'sha" carries the sense of plurality.

"And they think" meaning the disbelievers think "that they are guided." It was also said: the disbelievers think the devils are guided, so they obey them.

"Until, when he comes to Us" (*jaa'anaa*, singular). Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read it in the singular, meaning the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection. The rest read *jaa'anaa* in the dual, meaning the disbeliever and his companion, who have been placed in one chain. Then the disbeliever says: ﴿O, would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts!﴾ meaning the east of winter and the east of summer, as He says: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [[verse 17 of al-Rahman]] [al-Rahman: 17]. Muqatil's view is similar.

Although the reading in the singular seems to refer to one, the meaning applies to both, since this is known from what follows, as the poet said:

*And an eye with a large, firm, bright gaze, / whose lids were split from behind.* [[The verse is by Imru' al-Qays. *Hadrah*: full, firm; it is said also wide and protruding. *Badrah*: quick to look, and it is said complete like the full moon.]]

Muqatil said: the disbeliever wishes that the distance between them were the distance from the east of the longest day of the year to the east of the shortest day of the year. For this reason He said "the distance of the two easts." Al-Farra' said: He meant the east and the west, and He gave precedence to the name of one of them, as one says: *al-qamarani* for the sun and the moon, *al-'umaran* for Abu Bakr and 'Umar, *al-basratan* for Kufa and Basra, and *al-'asran* for the morning and the afternoon. A poet said:

*We took, against you, the horizons of the sky, / for us are its two moons and the rising stars.*

Abu 'Ubaydah recited for Jarir:

*The Messenger of God would not have approved their deed, / nor the two 'Umars, Abu Bakr and 'Umar.*

Sibawayh recited:

*Enough of me for the support of the two wicked ones, enough.*

He means 'Abd Allah and Mus'ab, the two sons of al-Zubayr, though the kunya of 'Abd Allah is Abu Khubayb.

"Then how evil is the companion" meaning: how evil a companion you are, because he leads him to the Fire. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: when the disbeliever is raised, he is joined with his companion from the devils, and he does not part from him until he brings him to the Fire.

"Then how evil is the companion" meaning: how evil a companion you are, because he leads him to the Fire. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: when the disbeliever is raised, he is joined with his companion from the devils, and he does not part from him until he brings him to the Fire.

"Their saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you did wrong﴾. "Idh" (since) is a substitute (badal) for "al-yawm" (today). That is, God says to the disbelievers: it will not benefit you today, since you associated partners with Him in the world, this speech, which is the saying of the disbeliever: "Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts" — that is, regret will not benefit you today. "Innakum" with a kasra, "fi al-adhabi mushtarikun" (you are sharing in the punishment). This is the reading of Ibn Amir according to one of the variant transmissions from him. The rest read it with a fatha. It is in the position of the nominative, its implied sense being: "And your sharing in the punishment will not benefit you today, because each one of you has his greatest share of it." God, exalted is He, informed that He withheld from the people of the Fire the consolation (ta'assi) that people of calamities in the world seek, for the consolation is something the people of the world take comfort in, so one of them says: "In affliction and calamity I have an example (uswah)," and so that calms some of his grief, as al-Khansa' said:

"Were it not for the abundance of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself.
And they do not weep like my brother, but I console my soul over him by consolation."

So in the Hereafter, consolation did not benefit them at all, because they were occupied with the punishment. Muqatil said: "It will not benefit you today, the excuse and the regret, because your companions and you, in the punishment, are sharing, just as you shared in disbelief."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 40:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Can you make the deaf hear, or guide the blind,﴾ O Muhammad, ﴿and those who are in manifest error?﴾ That is, it is not for you to do so. So do not let your breast be constricted if they disbelieve. In this there is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ).

In it there is also a refutation of the Qadariyyah (the Qadariyyah, a early theological school that denied divine predestination) and others, and that guidance, rectitude and abandonment (al-khidhlan) in the heart are the creation of Allah the Exalted: He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verses 41–42:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So whether We take you away﴾, meaning, We will bring you out of Makkah because of the harm of the Quraysh [[the phrase "min adha Quraysh" is omitted in manuscript N]]. ﴿Indeed, We will take vengeance upon them. Or We will show you that which We have promised them﴾, which is the vengeance upon them during your lifetime, ﴿for indeed, We are Omnipotent over them﴾. Ibn Abbas said: Allah has indeed shown him that on the day of Badr, and this is the view of most of the exegetes (mufassirun). Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it concerns the people of Islam, meaning the trials that occurred after the Prophet ﷺ. And ﴿We will take you away﴾ according to this view means ﴿We will cause you to die﴾. After the Prophet ﷺ there was severe retribution, so Allah honored His Prophet ﷺ and took him away, and did not show him [the retribution] among his community except what would gladden his eye, and He left the retribution after him. There is no prophet except that he has been shown the retribution among his community. It is related that the Prophet ﷺ was shown what his community would suffer after him, and he remained withdrawn, never smiling broadly, until he met Allah, mighty and majestic. It is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When Allah wills good for a community, He takes its prophet before it and makes him a forerunner and a predecessor for it. And when Allah wills punishment for a community, He punishes it while its prophet is still alive, so that his eye is comforted, because they denied him and disobeyed his command."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 43–44:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So hold fast to what has been revealed to you﴾. He means the Qur'an, even if those who denied it denied it. "Indeed, you are on a straight path" leads you to God, His good pleasure and His reward. "And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people": that is, the Qur'an is an honour for you and for your people from Quraysh, since it was revealed in their language and upon a man from among them. Its parallel is: ﴿We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya: 10], meaning your honour.[[Verse 10, surah al-Anbiya.]] So the Qur'an descended in the tongue of Quraysh and addressed them, and the people of all languages came to need their tongue. Everyone who believed in it became dependent upon them, because the people of every language needed to take it from their language in order to grasp the meaning intended by its commands, prohibitions and all its reports. Thus they were honoured over the rest of the people of languages, and for this reason it was called Arabic (ʿarabiyy). It is also said: it is an explanation for you and your community of what you need. It is also said: it is a reminder by which you recall the matters of religion and act upon them. It is also said: "And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people" means the caliphate, for it is among Quraysh and is not to be held by anyone other than them. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The people follow Quraysh in this matter: their Muslims follow their Muslims, and their disbelievers follow their disbelievers." Malik said: it is the saying of a man, "My father narrated to me from his father," related by Ibn Abi Salama from his father from Malik ibn Anas, as mentioned by al-Mawardi, al-Tha'labi and others. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "I have not found this rank in Islam for anyone except in Baghdad, where the Banu al-Tamimi say, 'My father narrated to me, who said, my father narrated to me,' up to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and through this their standing was elevated, people magnified their status, and the caliphate was entrusted to them." In the city of Peace (Baghdad) I saw the two sons of Abu Muhammad Rizq Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhab, Abu al-Faraj ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn al-Harith ibn al-Asad ibn al-Layth ibn Sulayman ibn Aswad ibn Sufyan ibn Yazid ibn Ukayna ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Tamimi, and they would say: "We heard our father Rizq Allah say: I heard my father say: I heard my father say: I heard my father say: I heard my father say: I heard my father say: I heard ʿAli ibn Abi Talib say," when he was asked about al-Hannan al-Mannan. He said: "al-Hannan is the one who turns toward whoever turns away from Him, and al-Mannan is the one who begins with bounty before being asked." The one who said "I heard ʿAli" was Ukayna ibn ʿAbd Allah, their highest ancestor. The stronger view is that what is meant by "And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people" is the Qur'an, for the speech is built upon it and the final outcome returns to it, and God knows best. Al-Mawardi said: regarding "and your people" there are two views: first, those who followed you from your community, said by Qatada and mentioned by al-Tha'labi from al-Hasan; second, your people from Quraysh, so it is asked, "From whom is this?" It is answered, "From the Arabs." It is asked, "From which Arabs?" It is answered, "From Quraysh," said by Mujahid. I say: the correct view is that it is an honour for whoever acts upon it, whether they were from Quraysh or from others. Ibn ʿAbbas narrated: The Prophet of God ﷺ came back from a military expedition or a campaign, and he called Fatima and said: "O Fatima, buy yourself from God, for I cannot avail you anything against God." He said the same to his wives, and said the same to his close kin. Then the Prophet of God ﷺ said: "The Banu Hashim are not the closest of people to my community; the closest of people to my community are the God-fearing. Quraysh are not the closest of people to my community; the closest of people to my community are the God-fearing. The Ansar are not the closest of people to my community; the closest of people to my community are the God-fearing. The clients are not the closest of people to my community; the closest of people to my community are the God-fearing. You are only from a man and a woman, and you are like the measure [[al-jimam (with three vowel forms): what rises above the rim of the measuring vessel.]] of the sa' (a measure); no one has any superiority over another except through piety." And from Abu Hurayra who said: the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Let people stop boasting of coal from the coals of Hell, or they will be more contemptible before God than the dung beetles that push filth with their noses. All of you are the children of Adam, and Adam was made of dust. Indeed God has removed from you the arrogance of the Jahiliyya and its pride in ancestors. People are either a pious believer or a wretched sinner." Al-Tabari transmitted both. More will come on this in al-Hujurat, God willing. "And you will be questioned": that is, about gratitude for it, said by Muqatil and al-Farra'. Ibn Jurayj said: that is, you and those with you will be questioned about what has been brought to you. It is also said: you will be questioned about what you did with it. The meanings are close.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 45:

Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the night journey (isra') from the Masjid al-Haram to the Masjid al-Aqsa, which is the Masjid of Bayt al-Maqdis, Allah sent Adam and those of the messengers born of him to him, and Jibril was with the Prophet (ﷺ). Jibril called the adhan, then gave the iqamah for the prayer, then said: "O Muhammad, go forward and lead them in prayer." When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had finished, Jibril said to him: [Ask, O Muhammad, those whom We sent before you of Our messengers: Did We appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Merciful?] The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: [I will not ask; I am content.] Ibn ʿAbbas said: They were seventy prophets, among them Ibrahim, Musa and ʿIsa (peace be upon them), and he did not ask them, because he was more knowing of Allah than they were.

In a narration other than that of Ibn ʿAbbas: They prayed behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in seven rows, the messengers being three rows and the prophets four. Directly behind the back of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah, on his right was Isma'il, on his left was Ishaq, then Musa, then the rest of the messengers. So he led them in two rakʿahs. When he turned away (the verb infatala means that he turned away from the prayer, i.e., departed from it), he stood and said: [My Lord has revealed to me that I should ask you: Has any one of you been sent who calls to the worship of other than Allah?] They said: "O Muhammad, we bear witness that we were all sent with one call: that there is no god but Allah, that what they worship besides Him is false, and that you are the Seal of the Prophets and the master of the messengers. This has become clear to us through your leading us, and that there is no prophet after you until the Day of Resurrection, except ʿIsa son of Maryam, for he is commanded to follow your path." Sa'id ibn Jubayr, concerning the words of the Most High, "And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers," said: He met the messengers on the night he was taken on the journey. Al-Walid ibn Muslim, concerning the words of the Most High, "And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers," said: I asked Khalid ibn Da'laj about this, and he related to me from Qatadah, who said: He asked them on the night he was taken on the journey; he met the prophets and met Adam and Malik, the keeper of the Fire. I say: This is the sound view in the interpretation of this verse, and the "min" that precedes "messengers" (rusulina) on this view is not superfluous.

Al-Mubarrad and a group of scholars said: The meaning is "and ask the nations of those whom We sent before you of Our messengers." It is related that in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is "and ask those to whom We sent Our messengers before you," and this is an explanatory reading, so the "min" here is superfluous. This is the view of Mujahid, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, ʿAta', al-Hasan, and also Ibn ʿAbbas, i.e., ask the believers among the People of the Two Books, the Torah and the Gospel. It was also said: The meaning is, "Ask us, O Muhammad, about the prophets whom We sent before you," so "ʿan" (about) has been omitted, and the pause on "rusulina" is complete on this view, then the interrogative begins in the manner of denial. It was also said: The meaning is "and ask the followers of those whom We sent before you of Our messengers," so the noun modified has been omitted. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is intended is his community. "Did We appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Merciful?" He spoke of the gods as he would speak of those who have reason, saying "yu'badun" (they are worshipped, in the masculine plural), and did not say tu'bad or yu'badna, because the gods were regarded by them as beings of reason, so the report about them took the form of a report about those who have reason. The reason for this command to ask is that the Jews and the polytheists said to the Prophet (ﷺ): What you have brought opposes what came before you. So Allah commanded him to ask the prophets by way of confirmation and affirmation, not because he was in doubt about it.

The commentators differed about the Prophet's (ﷺ) asking them, on two views. The first: that he asked them, and the messengers said: "We were sent with monotheism," as al-Waqidi related. The second: that he did not ask them, because of his certainty in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to the extent that Ibn Zayd related that Mika'il said to Jibril: "Did Muhammad ask you about that?" Jibril said: "He is too firm in faith and too great in certainty to ask about that." This meaning has already been mentioned in the two narrations, as we have described.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verses 46–52:**

Allah's words: ﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾. When Allah informed the Prophet ﷺ that He would avenge him against his enemy, and established the proof through the testimony of the prophets and the agreement of all of them on monotheism (tawhid), He confirmed this with the story of Musa and Fir'awn, what Fir'awn did of denial, and what befell him and his people of drowning and denial. That is: We sent Musa with the miracles, which were the nine signs, and he was denied. The good outcome was made his, and so it will be for you.

"Yadhakun" (they laugh) means mockery and derision. They deceived their followers into thinking that those signs were sorcery and illusion, and that they themselves were capable of producing them.

His words: "And We did not show them any sign except that it was greater than its sister." That is, the signs of Musa were among the greatest signs, and each one was greater than the one before it.

It was also said: "except that it was greater than its sister," because the first sign requires knowledge and the second requires knowledge, so the second is joined to the first and clarity increases. The meaning of "akhuwwah" (sisterhood) is resemblance and affinity, as one says: "this is the companion of this," meaning they are close in meaning.

"And We seized them with punishment" — that is, for their denial of those signs. This is like His saying: ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Fir'awn with years of drought and shortage of crops﴾ [al-A'raf: 130]. And the flood, the locusts, the lice and the frogs. These last signs were a punishment for them and signs for Musa. "So that they might return" from their disbelief.

"And they said: O sorcerer" — when they witnessed the punishment, they said, "O sorcerer." They called him by what they had been calling him before that, according to their habit. It was also said that they used to call scholars "sahirun" (sorcerers), so they addressed him with that as a form of honour. Ibn 'Abbas said: "O sorcerer" means "O scholar," and the sorcerer among them was a great man whom they revered, and sorcery was not a term of blame.

It was also said: "O you who overcame us with your sorcery." One says: "sahartuhu" for "sa'hartuhu" and "sahartuhu," meaning I overcame him by sorcery, like the Arab saying: "khasamtuhu fa-khasamtuhu," meaning I overcame him in dispute, and "fadaltuhu fa-fadaltuhu" and similar.

It is also possible that they meant by it the sorcerer in the literal sense, as a question, and so he did not blame them for this, in hope that they would believe.

Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywah and Yahya ibn Wathhab recited "Wayyuhu al-sahiru" without an alif, with the ha' vowelled with a damma. The reason for this is that the ha' was joined to what came before it, and it was obligated to take the damma of the yā' which the singular vocative requires. Al-Farra' cited:

*O heart, stubborn in its breathing,*
*turn away from the white, graceful, dark-lipped ones.*

Here he vowelled the ha' with a damma by analogy with the damma of the yā'. The meaning of this has already passed in "al-Nur" [see vol. 12, p. 238].

Abu 'Amr, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Yahya and al-Kisa'i stopped on "ayyuha" with an alif, according to the original form. The rest recited it without an alif, because it is written so in the codex (mushaf).

"Pray to your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you" — that is, by what He told us of His covenant with you: that if we believe, He will remove the punishment from us. So ask Him, and He will remove it from us. "Indeed we will be guided" — that is, in what is to come.

"So when We removed the punishment from them" — that is, he prayed and We removed it. "Behold, they broke their word" — that is, they broke the covenant they had made upon themselves, and did not believe.

It was also said: their saying "Indeed we will be guided" was a report from them about themselves of their faith, but when the punishment was removed from them, they apostatised.

His words: "And Fir'awn proclaimed among his people." It was said: when he saw those signs, he feared the people's inclination towards Musa, so he gathered his people and spoke. Here "nada" (proclaimed) means "qala" (said). This was stated by Abu Malik. It is possible that the great men of the Copts were with him, and he raised his voice with that among them, and then it spread among the masses of the Copts, as though he had been proclaimed among them. It was also said that he ordered someone to proclaim among his people. This was stated by Ibn Jurayj.

"He said: O my people, is not the kingdom of Egypt mine?" — that is, no one disputes it with me. It was said that he ruled forty farsakhs by forty farsakhs of it, as related by al-Nahhas. It was also said that by "kingdom" here he meant Alexandria.

"And these rivers flow beneath me" — meaning the rivers of the Nile, the majority of which are four: the Nahr al-Mulk, the Nahr Tulun, the Nahr Dimyat and the Nahr Tinis. [In the book Ruh al-Ma'ani by al-Alusi: "The rivers: the channels that come out of the blessed Nile, such as the Nahr al-Mulk, the Nahr Dimyat, and the Nahr Tinis, and perhaps the Nahr Tulun was among them at that time, but it was obliterated, so Ahmad ibn Tulun, king of Egypt in Islam, renewed it."]

Qatadah said: they were gardens and rivers flowing from beneath his palaces. It was also said: from beneath his throne. It was also said: "from beneath me" means my authority is executed over them without any worker. It was also said that when he held back his rein, the Nile held back from flowing. Al-Qushayri said: supernatural phenomena may appear through one who claims lordship, since distinguishing God from what is not God requires no supernatural act.

It was also said that the meaning of "And these rivers flow beneath me" is that the commanders, leaders and tyrants march beneath my banner. This was stated by al-Dahhak. It was also said that by "the rivers" he meant wealth, and expressed it by rivers because of its abundance and visibility. And his words "flow beneath me" mean: I distribute it among those who follow me, because the attraction and power lie in wealth, not in rivers.

"Will you not then see?" — my greatness, my power, and the weakness of Musa. It was also said: my power over your provision, and the inability of Musa.

The waw in "wa-hadhihi" (and these) may be a conjunction joining the rivers to "the kingdom of Egypt," and "tajri" (flow) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from them. It may also be the waw of the circumstantial clause, with the demonstrative as the subject (mubtada'), "al-anhar" (the rivers) as an adjective of the demonstrative, and "tajri" as the predicate of the subject.

The people of Madina, al-Bazzi and Abu 'Amr vowelled the yā' in "min tahti" (beneath me) with a fatha, and the rest made it sukun.

It is related of al-Rashid that when he recited it he said: "I will certainly appoint to it the best of my slaves," and he appointed al-Khasib, who was in a state of ablution. It is related of Abdullah ibn Tahir that he was appointed to it and went out to it, and when he approached it and its view met his eye, he said: "Is this the village about which Fir'awn boasted, to the point that he said, 'Is not the kingdom of Egypt mine?' By God, it is less in my estimation than that I should enter it!" And he turned his rein back.

Then he (Fir'awn) declared his state, saying: "Am I not better?" Abu 'Amr, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Yahya and al-Kisa'i stopped on "ayyuha" with an alif, according to the original form. The rest recited it without an alif, because it is written so in the codex (mushaf).

"Pray to your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you" — that is, by what He told us of His covenant with you: that if we believe, He will remove the punishment from us. So ask Him, and He will remove it from us. "Indeed we will be guided" — that is, in what is to come.

"So when We removed the punishment from them" — that is, he prayed and We removed it. "Behold, they broke their word" — that is, they broke the covenant they had made upon themselves, and did not believe.

It was also said: their saying "Indeed we will be guided" was a report from them about themselves of their faith, but when the punishment was removed from them, they apostatised.

His words: "And Fir'awn proclaimed among his people." It was said: when he saw those signs, he feared the people's inclination towards Musa, so he gathered his people and spoke. Here "nada" (proclaimed) means "qala" (said). This was stated by Abu Malik. It is possible that the great men of the Copts were with him, and he raised his voice with that among them, and then it spread among the masses of the Copts, as though he had been proclaimed among them. It was also said that he ordered someone to proclaim among his people. This was stated by Ibn Jurayj.

"He said: O my people, is not the kingdom of Egypt mine?" — that is, no one disputes it with me. It was said that he ruled forty farsakhs by forty farsakhs of it, as related by al-Nahhas. It was also said that by "kingdom" here he meant Alexandria.

"And these rivers flow beneath me" — meaning the rivers of the Nile, the majority of which are four: the Nahr al-Mulk, the Nahr Tulun, the Nahr Dimyat and the Nahr Tinis. [In the book Ruh al-Ma'ani by al-Alusi: "The rivers: the channels that come out of the blessed Nile, such as the Nahr al-Mulk, the Nahr Dimyat, and the Nahr Tinis, and perhaps the Nahr Tulun was among them at that time, but it was obliterated, so Ahmad ibn Tulun, king of Egypt in Islam, renewed it."]

Qatadah said: they were gardens and rivers flowing from beneath his palaces. It was also said: from beneath his throne. It was also said: "from beneath me" means my authority is executed over them without any worker. It was also said that when he held back his rein, the Nile held back from flowing. Al-Qushayri said: supernatural phenomena may appear through one who claims lordship, since distinguishing God from what is not God requires no supernatural act.

It was also said that the meaning of "And these rivers flow beneath me" is that the commanders, leaders and tyrants march beneath my banner. This was stated by al-Dahhak. It was also said that by "the rivers" he meant wealth, and expressed it by rivers because of its abundance and visibility. And his words "flow beneath me" mean: I distribute it among those who follow me, because the attraction and power lie in wealth, not in rivers.

"Will you not then see?" — my greatness, my power, and the weakness of Musa. It was also said: my power over your provision, and the inability of Musa.

The waw in "wa-hadhihi" (and these) may be a conjunction joining the rivers to "the kingdom of Egypt," and "tajri" (flow) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from them. It may also be the waw of the circumstantial clause, with the demonstrative as the subject (mubtada'), "al-anhar" (the rivers) as an adjective of the demonstrative, and "tajri" as the predicate of the subject.

The people of Madina, al-Bazzi and Abu 'Amr vowelled the yā' in "min tahti" (beneath me) with a fatha, and the rest made it sukun.

It is related of al-Rashid that when he recited it he said: "I will certainly appoint to it the best of my slaves," and he appointed al-Khasib, who was in a state of ablution. It is related of Abdullah ibn Tahir that he was appointed to it and went out to it, and when he approached it and its view met his eye, he said: "Is this the village about which Fir'awn boasted, to the point that he said, 'Is not the kingdom of Egypt mine?' By God, it is less in my estimation than that I should enter it!" And he turned his rein back.

Then he (Fir'awn) declared his state, saying: "Am I not better?" Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Sadi said: "am" (am) here means "bal" (rather) and is not a conjunction, according to the view of most of the exegetes. The meaning is: Fir'awn said to his people, "Rather, I am better than this one who is despised," that is, he has no honour, so he degrades himself in his needs because of his lowliness and weakness. "And he can hardly express himself clearly" — meaning the impediment that was in his tongue, as previously mentioned in "Ta Ha" [see vol. 11, p. 192].

Al-Farra' said: regarding "am" there are two possibilities. If you wish, you may make it an interrogative which is joined by "am" to a statement before it. If you wish, you may make it a coordinating particle upon his saying "Is not the kingdom of Egypt mine?" It was also said that it is superfluous (za'idah). Abu Zayd related from the Arabs that they treat "am" as superfluous, and the meaning is: I am better than this one who is despised.

Al-Akhfash said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the meaning is: "Will you not then see? Or will you see?" as he said:

*O gazelle of the sandy plain between Jalajil*
*and the dune, are you, or the mother of Salim?*

[The speaker is Dhu al-Rummah. Al-wa'sa': a soft sandy tract. Jalajil: a specific place. Al-naqa': a sand hill.]

That is: are you more beautiful, or the mother of Salim? Then he began and said: "I am better." Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: the meaning is "Will you not see? Or are you seers?" so "am" is coordinated with "Will you not see?" because the meaning of "am ana khayr" is "am ayyu tubsirun" (or which of you sees?), since when they say to him, "You are better than him," they are seers in his estimation.

It is related from 'Isa al-Thaqafi and Ya'qub al-Hadrami that they both stopped on "am," with the assumption that the estimate is "Will you not see? Or will you see?" and so the second "tubsirun" was omitted. It was also said: whoever stops on "am" treats it as superfluous, and it seems he stopped on "tubsirun" in "Will you not see?" Al-Khalil and Sibawayh do not regard the statement as complete at "tubsirun," because "am" requires connection with what precedes it. Some people said: stopping is on "Will you not see?", then one begins "am ana khayr," meaning "bal ana khayr" (rather, I am better). Al-Farra' cited:

*She appeared like the horn of the sun in the brilliance of forenoon,*
*and its form: am you are more graceful in the eye.*

Its meaning: rather, you are more graceful.

Al-Farra' mentioned that some reciters recited "amma ana khayr," and the meaning of this is: "am I not better?" It is related from Mujahid that he stopped on "am" and then began "ana khayr," and this has been mentioned.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 43, verse 53:

Allah's words ﴿So why are not bracelets of gold cast upon him?﴾ ("fa-lawla"), meaning: why not (hallā) ﴿bracelets of gold cast upon him﴾. He said this because it was the custom of the time and the dress of the people of nobility. Hafs read ﴿asworatun﴾ (أَسْوِرَةٌ) as the plural of siwār (سِوَارٌ), like khimār and akhmirah. Ubayy read ﴿asawiru﴾ (أَسَاوِرُ) as the plural of iswār (إِسْوَارٌ), and Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿asawīru﴾ (أَسَاوِيرُ). The rest read ﴿asworatun﴾ as the plural of al-asworah (الْأَسْوِرَةُ), which makes it a plural of a plural (jam' al-jam'). It is also possible that ﴿asawiratun﴾ (أَسَاوِرَةٌ) is the plural of iswār, with the ha' (هَاء) added in the plural in place of the ya' (يَاء), as in zanādīq and zanādiqah, and baṭārīq and baṭāriqah, and the like. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: the singular of asāwirah, asāwir and asāwīr is iswār, and it is a dialectal form of siwār. Mujahid said: when they invested a man with authority, they invested him with two bracelets and placed a gold collar around his neck as a sign of his lordship. So Pharaoh said: "Why has the Lord of Moses not cast upon him bracelets of gold, if he is truthful?"

﴿Or the angels came with him, accompanying him﴾: meaning, following one after another, according to Qatadah. Mujahid said: walking together. Ibn 'Abbas said: assisting him against those who oppose him. The meaning is: why did he not join to himself the angels whom he claims are with his Lord, so that he would be strengthened by them and they would carry out his command and prohibition, and that would be more awe-inspiring to hearts. Thus he gave his people the impression that the messengers of God should be like the messengers of kings in the visible world, and he did not know that the messengers of God are only supported by heavenly armies. Every intelligent person knows that God's protection of Moses, though he was alone and solitary, against Pharaoh with his many followers, and the support given to Moses through the staff and the white hand, were more eloquent than having bracelets or angels with him as helpers, according to the view of Muqatil, or as proof of his truthfulness, according to the view of al-Kalbi. This is not necessary, because the miracle is sufficient. It was possible that he would be denied even with the coming of the angels, just as he was denied in spite of the manifest signs. Pharaoh mentioned the angels as a report from the words of Moses, because one does not believe in the angels unless one knows their Creator.

**Allah's words: ﴿So he made light of his people⁠﴾.** Ibn al-A'rabi said: The meaning is: he made his people ignorant (fa-istajhala qawmahu), "so they obeyed him," because of the lightness of their minds and the scarcity of their reason. It is said: istakhaffahu al-faraḥ means "joy unsettled him" (azʿajahu). Istakhaffahu also means "he drove him to ignorance (al-jahl)." From this is Allah's words: ﴿And let not those who have no certainty make you light (lā yastakhiffannaka)⁠﴾ [al-Rum: 60]. It has also been said: he incited them with words, so they obeyed him in denying (the truth). It has also been said: "He made light of his people," meaning he found them light-minded (khafaf al-ʿuqul). But this does not indicate that they were obliged to obey him, so a distant implied element (idmar baʿid) must be assumed, its estimate being: he found them light-minded, so he called them to error, and they obeyed him. It has also been said: he made light of his people and overpowered them until they followed him; it is said istakhaffahu, contrary to istathqalahu (he found him burdensome), and istakhaffa bihi means he humiliated him. ﴿Indeed, they were a people of defiant transgression (qawman fasiqin)⁠﴾, meaning they were outside of obedience to Allah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 55:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them﴾. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: that is, they enraged Us and made Us angry. And 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from him: that is, they provoked Our displeasure (sakhat, lit. "displeasure/wrath"). Al-Mawardi said: their meanings differ, and the difference between them is that sakhat is the manifestation of dislike, while ghadab (anger) is the will to take vengeance.

Al-Qushayri said: al-asaf here means ghadab (anger), and anger from Allah is either the will to punish, in which case it belongs to the attributes of the Essence (sifat al-dhat), or the punishment itself, in which case it belongs to the attributes of the Act (sifat al-fi'l). This is the meaning of al-Mawardi's statement.

'Umar ibn Dharr said: O people who disobey Allah, do not be deceived by the length of Allah's forbearance toward you, and beware of His anger (asaf), for He said: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them﴾. It was also said: "ʾasafūnā" means they angered Our messengers and Our believing friends, such as the magicians and the Children of Israel. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who annoy Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 57] and ﴿those who wage war against Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33], meaning His friends and His messengers.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 56:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We made them a forerunner﴾, meaning: We made the people of Pharaoh a forerunner (salaf). Abu Mijlaz said: "salafan" is for whoever does their deeds, and "mathalan" (an example) is for whoever does their deeds. Mujahid said: "salafan" is a report to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and "mathalan" means a lesson (ibra) for them. Also from him: "salafan" is for the disbelievers of your people, who will precede them to the Fire. Qatadah said: "salafan" means toward the Fire, and "mathalan" means an admonition for those who come after them.

Salaf means one who has gone before. It is said: salafa yaslufu salafan, like talaba yatlubu talaban, meaning he went forward and passed on. And "salafa lahu 'amalun salih" means a good deed went ahead for him. "Al-qawm al-silaf" means the people who have gone before, and the salaf of a man are his forefathers who have gone before; the plural is aslaf and sullaf.

The reading of the common people is "salafan" (with a fatha on the sin and the lam), the plural of salif, like khadim and khadam, rasid and rasad, and haris and haras. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "sulufan" (with a damma on the sin and the lam). Al-Farra' said: it is the plural of salif, like sarir and surur. Abu Hatim said: it is the plural of salaf, like khashab and khushub, and thamar and thumur, and their meanings are one. Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Alqamah, Abu Wa'il, al-Nakha'i and Humayd ibn Qays read "sulafan" (with a damma on the sin and a fatha on the lam), the plural of sulfah, meaning an advanced group. Al-Mu'arrij and al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "salafan" is the plural of sulfah, like ghurfah and ghuraf, turfah and turaf, and zulmah and zulam.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 57:

When Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: Did We appoint gods other than the Most Merciful to be worshipped?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 45], the polytheists clung to the matter of ʿĪsā (Jesus) and said: "Muhammad only wants us to take him as a god, just as the Christians took ʿĪsā ibn Maryam as a god." This was said by Qatadah. A similar account comes from Mujahid, who said: "Quraysh said: 'Muhammad wants us to worship him just as the people of ʿĪsā worshipped ʿĪsā,' so Allah revealed this verse."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: It refers to the debate of ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zibaʿrā with the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the matter of ʿĪsā. The one who coined this example was ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zibaʿrā al-Sahmi while he was still in disbelief, when Quraysh said to him that Muhammad was reciting: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98], and he said: "If I had been present, I would have refuted him." They said: "And what would you have said to him?" He said: "I would have said: 'This is al-Masih, whom the Christians worship, and the Jews worship ʿUzayr. Are these two from the fuel of Hell?'" Quraysh was amazed at his statement, and they considered that he had been defeated. That is the meaning of His saying "yasuddūn." Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us, they will be kept far away from it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 101].

Had Ibn al-Zibaʿrā reflected on the verse, he would not have objected to it, because he said "what you worship" (mā taʿbudūna) and did not say "whom you worship" (man taʿbudūna). He meant idols and the like, which do not reason, and he did not mean al-Masih or the angels, even though they were worshipped. This has already been discussed at the end of Surat al-Anbiya [see vol. 11, p. 343 onward].

Ibn ʿAbbas also narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Quraysh: "O assembly of Quraysh, there is no good in anyone who is worshipped besides Allah." They said: "Do you not claim that ʿĪsā was a servant of Allah and a righteous servant? If it is as you claim, then he was worshipped besides Allah!" So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And when the son of Maryam is cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it [with clamor]﴾, meaning they raise a clamor like the clamor of camels when loads are put on them.

Naafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir and al-Kisaʾi read "yaṣuddūn" (with a damma on the ṣād), and its meaning is "they turn away," as said by al-Nakhaʿi. The rest read it with a kasra. Al-Kisaʾi said: "Both are dialects, like yaʿrishūn and yaʿrushūn, and yanimmūn and yanummūn, and its meaning is 'they clamor.'" Al-Jawhari said: "ṣadda yaṣuddu ṣadīdan" means he clamored. It was also said that the damma form comes from ṣudūd (turning away), which is aversion, and the kasra form from dajīj (clamor); this was said by Qutrub. Abu ʿUbayd said: "If it were from turning away from the truth, it would be: 'idhā qawmuka ʿanhu yaṣuddūn.'" Al-Farraʾ said: "Both are the same: minhu and ʿanhu." Ibn al-Musayyab said: yaṣuddūn means yaḍijjūn (they clamor). Al-Dahhak said: yaʿijjūn (they cry out). Ibn ʿAbbas said: yaḍḥakūn (they laugh). Abu ʿUbayda said: whoever reads with a damma, its meaning is yaʿdilūn (they deviate), so the meaning is: out of inclination they deviate. "Yaṣuddūn" is not transitive with min; and whoever reads with a kasra, its meaning is yaḍijjūn, so "min" is connected to "yaṣuddūn," and the meaning is: they clamor because of it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Are our gods better, or is he?"﴾ That is: "Are our gods better, or is Jesus?" So said al-Suddi.

He also said: They disputed with him and said, "Everyone who is worshipped besides Allah is in the Fire. So we are content for our gods to be with Jesus, the angels and 'Uzayr." Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us, they will be kept far from it﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:101], and the verse continues.

Qatadah said: "﴿Or is he?﴾" means Muhammad (ﷺ).

In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud it is: ﴿Are our gods better, or is this one?﴾ This supports the view of Qatadah. It is an interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqrir, a question that asserts a point by eliciting agreement) that their gods are better.

The Kufans and Ya'qub read أَآلِهَتُنا with both hamzas pronounced fully (tahqiq, "making the hamza clear"), while the rest softened the second hamza (talyin, "making it easy"). This has already been discussed.

﴿They did not cite it to you except as a matter of contention﴾. Jadalan (جَدَلًا) is an accusative of state (hal), meaning "contentiously," i.e., "argumentatively." The meaning is: they did not cite this example to you except out of a desire to dispute, because they knew that what is meant by "the fuel of Hell" (hasab Jahannam) is what they had taken as gods of lifeless things (al-mawat). ﴿Rather, they are a quarrelsome people﴾, disputing with falsehood.

In Sahih al-Tirmidhi, on the authority of Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No people went astray after being guided to what they were upon, except that they were given to disputation." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿They did not cite it to you except as a matter of contention. Rather, they are a quarrelsome people﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 59–60:

Allah's statement: ﴿He was but a servant upon whom We bestowed favour﴾. That is, Isa was only a servant upon whom Allah bestowed prophethood, and He made him a sign (mathal) for the Children of Israel, that is, an ayah and a lesson (ibrah) by which the power of Allah the Exalted is to be inferred. For Isa was born without a father. Then there was given to him, from the raising of the dead, the healing of the blind and the leper, and all kinds of illnesses, what was not given to anyone else in his time, even though the Children of Israel at that time were the best of creation and the most beloved to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while the rest of mankind was below them; there was no one with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, like them. It is also said: the one meant by "the servant upon whom favour was bestowed" is Muhammad (ﷺ), but the first view is more apparent. ﴿And if We willed, We would have made from among you﴾, that is, instead of you, ﴿angels, who would succeed you on the earth﴾. This was said by al-Suddi, and similar is reported from Mujahid, who said: angels who would populate the earth in your place. Al-Azhari said: "min" may indicate substitution (li-l-badal), based on this verse. I say: this meaning has already been mentioned at [[see vol. 8, p. 141]] in "Bara'ah" and elsewhere. It is also said: if We willed, We would have made from among mankind angels, even though this is not the customary way; the substances are one genus and the difference lies in attributes. The meaning is: if We willed, We would have settled the angels in the earth, and there is no honour in our settling them in heaven such that they would be worshipped or be called the daughters of Allah. The meaning of "yakhlifun" is that some of them succeed others, as related from Ibn Abbas.

Allah's statement: ﴿He was but a servant upon whom We bestowed favour﴾. That is, Isa was only a servant upon whom Allah bestowed prophethood, and He made him a sign (mathal) for the Children of Israel, that is, an ayah and a lesson (ibrah) by which the power of Allah the Exalted is to be inferred. **Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 43 (al-Zukhruf), verses 61–62**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed it is a sign (ʿilm) of the Hour, so do not be in doubt about it﴾. Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: it means the Qur'an, because it indicates that the Hour is near, or because through it the Hour and its terrors and conditions are known. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Qatadah also said: it refers to the descent of ʿIsa (peace be upon him), and that is among the signs of the Hour, because God sends him down from heaven shortly before the Hour arises, just as the emergence of the Dajjal (the Antichrist) is among the signs of the Hour.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Hurayrah, Qatadah, Malik ibn Dinar and al-Dahhak read "wa-innahu la-ʿilmun lil-sāʿah" (with fatha on the ʿayn and the lam), meaning an indication (amarah). It has been narrated from ʿIkrimah the reading "wa-innahu la-lʿilmu" (with two lams), but that contradicts the codices (al-maṣāhif).

It is narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud who said: On the night the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he met Ibrahim, Musa and ʿIsa (peace be upon them), and they discussed the Hour. They began with Ibrahim and asked him about it, but he had no knowledge of it. Then they asked Musa, and he had no knowledge of it either. So the matter was referred to ʿIsa ibn Maryam, who said: "I was given a covenant concerning what is before its appointed time, but as for its appointed time, none knows it except God, Mighty and Majestic." Then he mentioned the emergence of the Dajjal, and said: "Then I will descend and kill him." And he related the hadith. Ibn Majah recorded it in his Sunan. And in Sahih Muslim: [Then while he – meaning the Dajjal – is [in that state], God sends the Messiah, the son of Maryam, and he descends at the white minaret east of Damascus, between two garments dyed with saffron (mahrudatayn) [i.e., two pieces or two outer garments], placing his palms on the wings of two angels. When he lowers his head, drops fall from it, and when he raises it, there flow from it pearls like pearls. No disbeliever who smells his breath will live, and his breath reaches as far as his sight reaches. He pursues him until he overtakes him at the gate of Lud (Lud, with a damma and shaddah: a village near Bayt al-Maqdis in the regions of Palestine), and kills him...] – the hadith. Al-Tha'labi, al-Zamakhshari and others transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: [ʿIsa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) will descend from heaven upon a mound of the Holy Land called Afiq,

between two lightly yellowed garments (mumassaratayn) [the mumassarah of garments is one with a light yellowish tinge], his head hair anointed, and in his hand a spear with which he will kill the Dajjal. He will come to Bayt al-Maqdis while the people are at the ʿAsr prayer and the imam is leading them. The imam will step back, and ʿIsa will advance him and pray behind him according to the law of Muhammad (ﷺ). Then he will kill the swine, break the cross, destroy the churches and synagogues, and kill the Christians except those who believe in him.] Khalid narrated from al-Hasan that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: [The prophets are half-brothers (ʿallat), their mothers are different but their religion is one, and I am the closest of people to ʿIsa ibn Maryam, for there is no prophet between me and him, and he is the first to descend. Al-Mawardi said: Ibn ʿIsa related from some people that they said: when ʿIsa descends, the obligation of legal duty (taklif) will be lifted, lest he be a messenger in that age commanding and forbidding on behalf of God. This view is rejected for three reasons: among them the hadith; and because the continuation of the world requires legal duty in it; and because he will descend commanding what is right and forbidding what is wrong. There is nothing objectionable in God's command to him being limited to supporting Islam, enjoining it and calling to it.

I say: It is established in Sahih Muslim and Ibn Majah from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: [ʿIsa ibn Maryam will certainly descend as a just judge, and he will certainly break the cross, kill the swine, abolish the jizyah, and camels will be left unattended, no one will pursue them, rancour, hatred and envy will disappear, and he will call people to wealth, but no one will accept it.] And from him, he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: [How will you be when the son of Maryam descends among you and your imam is from among you?] [and in one narration] [he will lead you from among you]. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verses 63–64:

Allah's statement: ﴿And when Jesus came with clear proofs﴾. Ibn Abbas said: he means the raising of the dead, the healing of the sick, the creating of birds, the table spread (al-ma'idah), and other such things, and informing them of many unseen matters. Qatadah said: "the clear proofs" here means the Injil (Gospel). ﴿He said: I have come to you with wisdom﴾, that is, prophethood. This was said by al-Suddi. Ibn Abbas said: it is knowledge of what leads to good and restrains from evil. It was also said that it is the Injil. This was mentioned by al-Qushayri and al-Mawardi.

﴿And that I may make clear to you some of that about which you differ﴾. Mujahid said: [this refers to] the alteration of the Tawrat (Torah). al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "that I may make clear to you in the Injil some of that about which you differ concerning the alteration of the Tawrat." Mujahid said: he made clear to them in matters other than the Injil whatever they needed. It was also said: he made clear to them some of what they had differed about from the rulings of the Tawrat according to what they asked him. It is permissible that they differed about other things besides these which they did not ask him about. It was also said: after the death of Musa, the Children of Israel differed about some matters of their religion and some matters of their worldly affairs, so he made clear to them the matter of their religion.

The school of Abu Ubaydah holds that "some" (al-ba'd) means "all" (al-kull). From this is Allah's statement: ﴿Some of what He promises you will befall you﴾ [Ghafir: 28]. al-Akhfash recited the verse of Labid:

Often I leave places when I do not like them,
or when the death-clinging seizes some souls and their pigeons (i.e., their lives).

Death does not cling to some souls and not others. The word for death is also called 'alūq and 'allaqah. al-Mufaddal al-Bakri said:

A woman asking about Tha'labah ibn Sayyar,
and the 'alūq has clung to Tha'labah.

Muqatil said: it is like His statement: ﴿And to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 50]. He means what was made lawful in the Injil that had been forbidden in the Tawrat, such as camel meat, fat from every animal, and catching fish on the Sabbath day.

﴿So fear Allah﴾, that is, beware of shirk (associating partners with Allah) and worship none but Allah alone. If this is the statement of Jesus, then how could it be permissible for him to be a god or the son of a god?

﴿And obey me﴾ in what I call you to of tawhid (affirmation of Allah's oneness) and other matters.

﴿Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path﴾, that is, the worship of Allah is a straight path, and whatever else is crooked, and does not lead its traveler to the truth.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verses 65–66:

Allah's words: ﴿So the factions differed among themselves﴾. Qatadah said: it means among themselves, that is, among the people of the earlier communities. There are two opinions about them. The first is that they are the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, some of whom opposed others. This was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi. The second is that the Christian sects, namely the Nestorians, the Melkites and the Jacobites (al-Ya'aqibah), differed concerning Jesus. The Nestorians said: he is the son of God. The Jacobites said: he is God. The Melkites said: he is the third of three, one of whom is God. This was said by al-Kalbi and Muqatil, and this has already been discussed in Surah Maryam [[See vol. 11, pp. 106, 108.]]. ﴿So woe to those who did wrong﴾, that is, those who disbelieved and associated partners with Allah, as in Surah Maryam [[See vol. 11, pp. 106, 108.]]. ﴿From the torment of a painful day﴾, that is, a day whose torment is painful. Similar to this is the expression "a sleeping night", meaning one in which people sleep. ﴿Do they await﴾ means the factions do not await anything ﴿except the Hour﴾, meaning the Resurrection, ﴿that it will come upon them suddenly﴾, that is, unexpectedly, ﴿while they do not perceive﴾, that is, they are not aware. This has been mentioned in more than one place [[See vol. 1, p. 197, second or third edition.]]. It has also been said: the meaning is that the polytheists of the Arabs await nothing except the Hour. On this reading, "the factions" are those among the polytheists who united against the Prophet ﴿ﷺ﴾ and denied him. This connects with His words: ﴿They did not set it forth to you except as a dispute﴾ [[Verse 58 of this surah.]] [Az-Zukhruf: 58].
