**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 43, verse 67:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The intimate friends that Day﴾, meaning the Day of Resurrection. "Some of them to others are enemies," that is, enemies: some of them are hostile to others and curse one another. "Except the righteous" (al-muttaqin): they are friends in this world and in the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others said this.

Al-Naqqash narrated that this verse was revealed concerning Umayya ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi and 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, who were close friends. 'Uqba used to sit with the Prophet (ﷺ). The Quraysh said, "'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt has become a convert (sabaʾa)." Umayya said to him, "My face is forbidden to your face (i.e., I will not speak to you) if you meet Muhammad and do not spit in his face." 'Uqba did so. The Prophet (ﷺ) then vowed to kill him, and he killed him on the day of Badr by sabran (the term means tying a person and executing him in cold blood). Umayya was killed in the battle, and this verse was revealed concerning them.

al-Tha'labi (may Allah be pleased with him) mentioned in regard to this verse [[the text between the brackets is missing from manuscript H]] that he said: There were two believing friends and two disbelieving friends. One of the believers died, and he said: "O Lord, so-and-so used to command me to obey You and Your Messenger, he used to enjoin good upon me and forbid me evil, and he would inform me that I would meet You. O Lord, do not let him go astray after me, guide him as You guided me, and honor him as You honored me." When his believing friend died, Allah brought the two together, and Allah the Exalted said: "Let each of you praise the other." The one says: "O Lord, he used to command me to obey You and Your Messenger, to enjoin good upon me and forbid me evil, and he would inform me that I would meet You." Allah the Exalted says: "What a excellent friend, brother and companion he was."

He said: One of the two disbelievers dies, and he says: "O Lord, so-and-so used to forbid me from obeying You and Your Messenger, he used to command me to do evil and forbid me good, and he would inform me that I would not meet You. So I ask You, O Lord, not to guide him after me, and to let him go astray as You let me go astray, and to humiliate him as You humiliated me." When his disbelieving friend dies, Allah the Exalted says to them both: "Let each of you praise the other." He says: "O Lord, he used to command me to disobey You and Your Messenger, he used to command me to do evil and forbid me good, and he would inform me that I would not meet You. So I ask You to multiply the punishment upon him." Allah the Exalted says: "What a wretched companion, brother and friend you were." Then each of them curses his companion.

I say: The verse is general, applying to every believer and God-fearing person, and every disbeliever and misguided person.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 68:

Muqatil said, and al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated it from his father: A caller will call out in the open plains (al-'arasat), "O My servants, no fear shall be upon you this Day," and the people of the plain will raise their heads. Then the caller will say, "Those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims," and the people of the (other) religions will lower their heads, except the Muslims.

al-Muhasibi (d. 243 AH) mentioned in al-Ri'aya: It has been related in this hadith that the caller will call out on the Day of Resurrection, "O My servants, no fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve," and the creatures will raise their heads, saying, "We are the servants of Allah." Then he will call a second time, "Those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims," and the disbelievers will lower their heads, while the monotheists remain with their heads raised. Then he will call a third time: ﴿Those who believed and were God-conscious﴾ [Yunus: 63], and the people of major sins will lower their heads, while the people of God-consciousness remain with their heads raised. He has removed from them fear and grief as He promised them, for He is the Most Generous of the generous, who does not forsake His friend nor abandon him in the time of ruin.

And it has been read "Ya 'ibad" (O servants) [with a short vowel on the final letter, in the vocative form].

al-Zajjaj said: "alladhina" is in the accusative as an adjective (na't) to "ibadi," because "ibadi" is a vocative with a possessive suffix (munada mudaf).

It is also said: "alladhina amanu" is either a predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), or a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, its implied sense being: "They are those who believed," or "Those who believed, it will be said to them: 'Enter the Garden.'"

Abu Bakr and Zirr ibn Hubaysh read "ya ibadi" with a fatha on the ya' and its retention in both states (pausal and connected). For this reason Nafi', Ibn Amir, Abu Amr and Ruways read it with the ya' sukun in both states. The rest omitted it in both states, because it was written with the ya' only in the codices of the people of Syria and Medina and not elsewhere.

"Udkhulu al-jannah" means: it will be said to them, "Enter the Garden," or: "O My servants who believed, enter the Garden."

"Antum wa azwajukum": the Muslim women in this world. It is also said: your companions among the believers. It is also said: your wives from the wide-eyed houris.

"Tuhbarun": you will be honored, as said by Ibn Abbas, and honor is in rank. Al-Hasan said: you will be delighted, and delight is in the heart. Qatadah said: you will be blessed with comfort, and comfort is in the body. Mujahid said: you will be gladdened, and gladness is in the eye. Ibn Abi Najih said: you will be amazed, and wonder here means perceiving what is novel and delightful. Yahya ibn Abi Kathir said: it is the enjoyment of listening (to music). This has already passed in "al-Rum."

**Issue 1:** Al-Qurtubi's commentary on the verse, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, on Surah 43, verse 71.

There are four issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will be served with dishes of gold and goblets﴾. That is, for them in Paradise there are foods and drinks, which will be brought around to them in dishes of gold and goblets. He did not mention the foods and drinks, because it is known that there is no sense in serving dishes and goblets to them unless there is something in them. He mentioned gold with the dishes and dispensed with repeating it for the goblets, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and the men who remember Allah much and the women who remember﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 35]. [[Verse 35 of Surah al-Ahzab. See vol. 14, p. (185).]]

In the *Sahihayn* (the two Sahihs), on the authority of Hudhayfah, that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "Do not wear silk or brocade, do not drink from vessels of gold and silver, and do not eat from their dishes, for they are for them (the unbelievers) in this world and for you in the Hereafter." [[His saying "from their dishes" is in the same sense as His saying, Exalted is He: "And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them..." The pronoun refers to silver, and the ruling for gold follows by a stronger inference.]] It has already passed in Surah al-Hajj [[See vol. 12, p. 29.]] that whoever eats from these two in this world, or wears silk in this world, and does not repent, is forbidden that in the Hereafter with a permanent prohibition. And Allah knows best.

The commentators have said: The least exalted person in Paradise in rank will be attended by seventy thousand boys, with seventy thousand dishes of gold, in which he is served a meal. In each dish there is a kind of food that is not in the other. He eats from its last part as he eats from its first, and finds the taste of its last part as he finds the taste of its first; none resembles another. And he is given the same again. And the most exalted of them in rank will be attended every day by seven hundred thousand boys, with each boy carrying a dish of gold, in which there is a kind of food not in the others. He eats from its last part as he eats from its first, and finds the taste of its last part as he finds the taste of its first; none resembles another.

"And goblets": that is, and they will be attended with goblets, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And they will be attended with vessels of silver and goblets﴾ [Al-Insan: 15]. [[Verse 15 of Surah al-Insan.]]

Ibn al-Mubarak narrated, saying: Ma'mar informed us, on the authority of a man, on the authority of Abu Qilabah, who said: "They will be brought food and drink. When the last of that is brought to them, they will be given the pure drink, and their bellies will be made lean by it, and sweat will flow from their skins, more fragrant than the scent of musk." Then he recited: ﴿a pure drink﴾ [Al-Insan: 21].

In the Sahih of Muslim, on the authority of Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "The people of Paradise eat therein and drink, and they do not spit, nor urinate, nor defecate, nor blow their noses." They said: "Then what of the food?" He said: "Belching and perspiration like the perspiration of musk. They are inspired to glorify (tasbih), praise (tahmid) and magnify (takbir), [in one narration:] as they are inspired to breathe."

**The second issue:** The imams narrated from the hadith of Umm Salamah, on the authority of the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "He who drinks in vessels of gold and silver is only causing the fire of Hell to gurgle in his belly." And he said: "Do not drink in vessels of gold and silver, and do not eat from their dishes." This requires prohibition, and there is no disagreement about that.

People differed concerning using them for other purposes. Ibn al-Arabi said: The correct view is that it is not permissible for men to use them for anything, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ concerning gold and silk: "These two are forbidden to the males of my community and lawful to its females." The prohibition on eating and drinking from them indicates the prohibition of using them, because it is a kind of utensil, so it is not permitted, like eating and drinking. The reason for this is hastening the reward of the Hereafter [[In Ibn al-Arabi: "ajr" (reward).]], which applies equally to eating, drinking and all other forms of benefit. Also, the Prophet ﷺ said: "They are for them in this world and for us in the Hereafter," so he did not give us any share of them in this world.

**The third issue:** If a vessel is overlaid with these two metals or has a ring of them on it, Malik said: "I do not like drinking from it. Likewise a mirror with a silver ring on it; I do not like looking into it to see one's face." Anas had a vessel banded with silver, and he said: "I certainly gave the Prophet ﷺ to drink from it." Ibn Sirin said: It had an iron ring, and Anas wanted to put a silver ring on it, but Abu Talhah said: "I will not change anything that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made," so he left it.

**The fourth issue:** If it is not permissible to use them, it is not permissible to keep them, because what may not be used may not be kept, like an idol or a *tunbur* [[The tunbur: a musical instrument with a long neck and six brass strings, an arabicised word.]]. In the books of our scholars it is said that whoever breaks them must pay their value. This is a corrupt view, for breaking them is obligatory, so there is no price for their value. And it is not permissible to assess them for zakat in any way. Anything other than this is not worth considering.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿bi-sihaf (with dishes)﴾. Al-Jawhari said: The *suhfah* (dish) is like the *qas'ah* (bowl), and the plural is *sihaf*. Al-Kisa'i said: The largest of the bowls is the *jafnah*, then the *qas'ah*, which feeds ten people; then the *suhfah*, which feeds five; then the *mi'kalah*, which feeds two or three men; then the *suhayfah*, which feeds one man. The *sahifah* is a book, and its plurals are *suhuf* and *sahair*.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wa-akwab (and goblets)﴾. Al-Jawhari said: The *kub* is a cup without a handle, and its plural is *akwab*. Al-A'sha described wine saying: *Sirifiyyah* (a wine of the village of Sarifun, or because it was taken from the jar at that moment like warm milk fresh from the udder), its taste is pleasant, / having foam between goblet and jar.

Another poet [[He is Adi ibn Zayd.]] said:

Reclining, its doors clapping, / a servant moves about him with the goblet.

Qatadah said: The *kub* is round, short-necked and short-handled. The *ibriq* (ewer) is long-necked and long-handled. Al-Akhfash said: The *akwab* are ewers that have no spouts. Qutrub said: They are ewers that have no handles. Mujahid said: They are vessels with round mouths. Al-Suddi said: They are those that have no ears (handles). Ibn Aziz said: "Akwab" are ewers with neither handles nor spouts; its singular is *kub*. I say: This is the meaning of the words of Mujahid and al-Suddi, and it is the view of the lexicographers that they are those that have neither ears nor handles.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And therein is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in﴾. Al-Tirmidhi narrated, on the authority of Sulayman ibn Buraydah, on the authority of his father, that a man asked the Prophet ﷺ: "O Messenger of Allah, is there horses in Paradise?" He said: "Indeed Allah will admit you into Paradise, and you will not desire to be carried therein on a horse of red ruby which will fly with you in Paradise wherever you wish." He said: And he asked him, and a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, is there camels in Paradise?" He said: So he did not say to him what he had said to his companion. He said: "If Allah admits you into Paradise, there will be for you therein whatever your soul desires and your eye delights in." [[An addition from the Sunan of al-Tirmidhi.]]

The people of Medina, Ibn Amir and the people of Syria read: "wa-fiha ma tashtahihi al-anfus" (what the souls desire), while the rest read: "tashtahi al-anfus" (the souls desire). That is, the souls desire it. You say: "The one whom you struck, Zaid" (meaning: "the one whom you struck is Zaid"). "And the eyes delight in": You say: *ladha al-shay'u yaladhdhu ladhadhan wa-ladhadhatan* (the thing was delicious), and *ladhidhtu bi-l-shay'* (I found it delicious) — *alladhdhu* in the past with kasra and in the future with fatha — *ladhadhan wa-ladhadhatan*, meaning I found it delicious. *Iltadhadhtu bihi* and *taladhdhadhtu bihi* have the same meaning. That is, in Paradise there is what the eye finds delightful, so it is beautiful to look upon. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "And the eyes delight in" refers to looking at Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as in the report: "I ask You for the delight of looking at Your Face."

"And you therein will abide": remaining, eternal, because if it were to end, they would be displeased.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 72:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that is the Garden﴾, meaning: it will be said to them, "This is that Garden which was described to you in the world."

Ibn Khalawayh said: God indicated the Garden with "that" (tilka) and Hell with "this" (hadhihi), so as to instil fear through Hell and to reinforce the warning against it. He made it, by the use of the near indication, like something present that one is looking at. ﴿Which you have been made to inherit because of what you used to do.﴾

Ibn Abbas said: God created for every soul a garden and a fire. So the disbeliever inherits the fire of the Muslim, and the Muslim inherits the garden of the disbeliever. This has already been mentioned as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) report in the commentary on ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1], from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, and also in al-A'raf.[[See vol. 12, p. (108)]] [al-Mu'minun: 1] [[See vol. 7, p. (208)]]

Al-Fakihah (fruit) is well known, and its plural is al-fawakih (fruits); al-fakihani is the one who sells them. Ibn Abbas said: they are all kinds of fruit, fresh and dry; that is, for them in Paradise, besides food and drink, there is abundant fruit from which they eat. ﴿Fruit, abundant, of which they eat.﴾

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the criminals will abide forever in the punishment of Hell.﴾ When He mentioned the conditions of the people of Paradise, He also mentioned the conditions of the people of the Fire, in order to show the superiority of the obedient over the disobedient. ﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾, meaning that punishment will not be reduced for them. ﴿And they will be in it despairing﴾, meaning hopeless of mercy. It was also said: they will be silent in the silence of despair. This has already been discussed in "al-An'am" [[see vol. 6, p. 426]]. ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ with the punishment, ﴿but they were the wrongdoers﴾ against themselves through shirk.

It is permissible to read ﴿wa-lakin kānū hum al-ẓālimūna﴾ with the nominative ending on al-ẓālimūn, as a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate), and the whole clause is the khabar of kāna.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the criminals will abide forever in the punishment of Hell.﴾ When He mentioned the conditions of the people of Paradise, He also mentioned the conditions of the people of the Fire, in order to show the superiority of the obedient over the disobedient. ﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾, meaning that punishment will not be reduced for them. ﴿And they will be in it despairing﴾, meaning hopeless of mercy. It was also said: they will be silent in the silence of despair. This has already been discussed in "al-An'am" [[see vol. 6, p. 426]]. ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ with the punishment, ﴿but they were the wrongdoers﴾ against themselves through shirk.

It is permissible to read ﴿wa-lakin kānū hum al-ẓālimūna﴾ with the nominative ending on al-ẓālimūn, as a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate), and the whole clause is the khabar of kāna.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the criminals will abide forever in the punishment of Hell.﴾ When He mentioned the conditions of the people of Paradise, He also mentioned the conditions of the people of the Fire, in order to show the superiority of the obedient over the disobedient. ﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾, meaning that punishment will not be reduced for them. ﴿And they will be in it despairing﴾, meaning hopeless of mercy. It was also said: they will be silent in the silence of despair. This has already been discussed in "al-An'am" [[see vol. 6, p. 426]]. ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ with the punishment, ﴿but they were the wrongdoers﴾ against themselves through shirk.

It is permissible to read ﴿wa-lakin kānū hum al-ẓālimūna﴾ with the nominative ending on al-ẓālimūn, as a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate), and the whole clause is the khabar of kāna.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 43, verse 77:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they will call, "O Malik"﴾. He is the keeper of Hell (*khazin Jahannam*), whom Allah created for His wrath. When he restrains the Fire with a single roar, parts of it devour other parts. ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "وَنَادَوْا يَا مَالِ" (*wa-nadaw ya Mal*, "and they will call, O Mal"), but that is contrary to the *mushaf* (the standardized written copy of the Qur'an). Abu al-Darda' and Ibn Masʿud said: The Prophet (ﷺ) recited "وَنَادَوْا يَا مَالِ" with the lam only, meaning he apocopated the name (*tarkhim*, "shortening by deleting the final letters") and deleted the kaf. *Tarkhim* means deletion, and from it comes the shortening of a name in the vocative. It is the deletion of one or more letters from the end of the word. So you say of Malik: "Ya Mal"; of Harith: "Ya Har"; of Fatimah: "Ya Fatim"; of ʿAishah: "Ya ʿAishi"; of Marwan: "Ya Marw"; and so on. The poet said:

*O Harith, I will not be struck by you with a calamity*
*that no commoner or king before me has encountered.*

[[The verse is by Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma, from a poem addressed to al-Harith ibn Waraqa al-Sayda'i, who had raided the Banu ʿAbd Allah ibn Ghatafan, seized booty and the camels of Zuhayr, and taken his shepherd Yasar. Zuhayr demanded that they return what they had taken and threatened them with satire ... etc. See the Sharh Diwan Zuhayr, p. 164, published by Dar al-Kutub al-Misriyya.]]

Imru' al-Qays said:

*Harith, do you see a flash of lightning whose glimmer I show you,*
*like the flash of two hands in a dense, layered cloud?*

[[Another reading has "أصاح" (*aṣāḥ*). *Al-ḥabiy* is the cloud spread across the horizon, and *al-mukallal* is the layered one.]]

He also said:

*Fatimah, be patient, leave off some of this coyness,*
*and if you have resolved to cut me off, then do so graciously.*

[[Fatimah is the daughter of ʿUbayd ibn Thaʿlaba ibn ʿAmir. *Al-ṣirm* (with a ḍamma) means severance.]]

Another poet said: [[It is al-Farazdaq addressing Marwan ibn al-Hakam, who was governor of Medina. He had come to him praising him, but his reward was delayed ... *Al-ḥibaʾ* (with a kasra on the ḥa') means gift. The man attributed it to the she-camel while meaning himself, as a metaphor.

(Sharh al-Shawahid by al-Shantamari.)]]

*O Marw, my mount is held back,*
*hoping for a reward, and its master has not despaired.*

And in the authentic hadith: "Ayyu fulu, halumma" ("O so-and-so, come here"). For the apocopated noun you have two options. The first is to keep it as it was before the deletion. The second is to build it on a ḍamma, as in "Ya Zaydu," as if you had placed it in the position of the full form without regard to what was deleted.

Abu Bakr al-Anbari reported, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Marwazi narrated to us, saying: Muhammad, who is Ibn Saʿdan, narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Shuʿba, from al-Hakam ibn ʿUyayna, from Mujahid, who said: "We did not know what *al-Zukhruf* meant until we found it in the reading of ʿAbd Allah: 'a house of gold.'"

And we did not know "وَنَادَوْا يَا مَالِكُ" whether it was "يا مالِكُ" or "يا مَلَكُ" (with a fatha or a kasra on the lam), until we found it in the reading of ʿAbd Allah: "وَنَادَوْا يَا مَالِ," as an apocopation. [[The phrase "or ya malak" is missing from manuscripts N and Z.]]

Abu Bakr said: This hadith is not to be acted upon, because it is an interrupted chain (*maqtuʿ*), and a report of this kind is not accepted as a narration from the Messenger, peace be upon him. The Book of Allah is more deserving of caution, and falsehood must be negated from it.

I say: In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Safwan ibn Yaʿla, from his father, who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) reciting on the pulpit: 'وَنادَوْا يا مالِكُ لِيَقْضِ عَلَيْنا رَبُّكَ' (And they will call, 'O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us'), with the kaf retained."

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi said: It has reached me, or it was mentioned to me, that the people of the Fire sought help from the guardians (*khazana*), and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell, "Call upon your Lord to lighten for us one day of the punishment"﴾ [Ghafir: 49]. So they asked for one single day of lightening of punishment, and they were answered: ﴿Did there not come to you your messengers with clear proofs?" They said, "Yes." They said, "Then call. But the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error."﴾ [Ghafir: 50]. He said: When they despaired of what the guardians could do, they called upon Malik, who is over them, and whose station is in the middle of it, with bridges over which the angels of punishment pass. He sees its farthest part just as he sees its nearest. So they said: "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us." He said: They asked for death. He said: He remained silent toward them and did not answer them for eighty years. He said: A year is three hundred and sixty days, a month is thirty days, and a day is like a thousand years of what you count. Then after the eighty years he glanced at them and said: "Indeed, you will remain" (*innakum makithun*). And he mentioned the hadith. Ibn al-Mubarak narrated it.

In the hadith of Abu al-Darda' from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: [They will say, "Call upon Malik," and they will say, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us." He will say, "Indeed, you will remain."]

Al-Aʿmash said: I have been informed that between their supplication and Malik's answer to them is a thousand years. Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: They say that, and he does not answer them for a thousand years, then he says, "Indeed, you will remain."

Mujahid and Nawf al-Bikali said: Between their calling and his answering them is a hundred years.

ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr said: Forty years. Ibn al-Mubarak narrated it.

It may be that this is from the words of Malik (the angel of hell) to them, meaning: you will remain in the Fire because We came to you in the world with the truth and you did not accept it. It may also be that it is from Allah's speech to them today, meaning: We made the proofs clear to you and sent the messengers to you. "But most of you" — Ibn 'Abbas said: "But most of you" means "but all of you." It was also said: by the majority he meant the leaders and commanders among them, while as for the followers, they had no influence. "Against the truth" means against Islam and the religion of Allah, "are averse."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 79:

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning their plotting with deceit against the Prophet ﷺ in Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of the Quraysh), when their decision settled on what Abu Jahl had suggested to them: that one man from every tribe should come forward so that they would all share in killing him, and thus the demand for his blood would be weakened. Then this verse was revealed, and Allah destroyed all of them at Badr. "Abramu" means they made firm, decided. Al-ibram (the act of making firm) is al-ihkam (making solid). "Abramtu al-shay'" means I made the thing firm. "Abrama al-fatil" means he made the twisting firm, and that is the second twisting, while the first is called sahil, as he said:

... min sahilin [[This is the second half of a line by Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma. The line, as in his Diwan, is:

Yaminan la-ni'ma al-saydani wajadtuma ... 'ala kulli hal min sahilin wa mubrami.

Al-sahil is the yarn that has not been twisted.]] wa mubramin

So the meaning is: "Or have they made a firm plot? Then We are the ones who make a firm plot against them," said Ibn Zayd and Mujahid. Qatadah said: "Or have they agreed upon denial? Then We are the ones who agree upon the recompense of resurrection." Al-Kalbi said: "Or have they decided a matter? Then We are the ones who decide against them with punishment." Here "am" carries the meaning of "bal" (rather). It was also said that "am abramu" is coordinated with His saying ﴿Did We appoint gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?﴾ [[Verse 45 of this surah.]] [al-Zukhruf: 45]. It was also said: meaning, "We have indeed brought you the truth, but you did not listen; or they did listen but turned away, because within themselves they had made firm a matter whose punishment they felt secure from."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 80:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private talk?﴾ That is, what they keep hidden within themselves and confer about among themselves. ﴿Yes,﴾ We hear and We know. ﴿And Our messengers are with them, recording.﴾ That is, the guardian angels with them are writing down about them.

It is narrated that this was revealed concerning three men who were between the Ka'bah and its curtains. One of them said: "Do you think that Allah hears our speech?" The second said: "If we speak aloud He hears, and if we speak in secret He does not hear." The third said: "If He hears when we make it public, then He hears when we keep it secret." This was related by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. This same meaning has already passed from Ibn Mas'ud in surah "Fussilat" [[see vol. 15, p. (351)]].

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers.﴾ Its meaning has been disputed. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: the meaning is "There was not for the Most Merciful a son," so "in" (in) here means "ma" (not), the sentence is complete on this reading, and then one begins with "then I am the first of the worshippers," that is, the first of the monotheists among the people of Makkah, on the basis that He has no son. The pause on "al-'Abidin" (the worshippers) is complete. It was also said: the meaning is, "Say, O Muhammad, if it were established that God has a son, then I would be the first to worship His son, but it is impossible that He should have a son." This is like what you say to one you are debating: "If what you said is proven by evidence, then I am the first to believe it," which is an exaggeration in deeming it unlikely, meaning there is no way to believe it. This is a softening of speech, like His saying: ﴿And indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba: 24]. The meaning on this view is: "Then I am the first of the worshippers of that son, because honouring the son is honouring the father." Mujahid said: the meaning is, "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first to worship Him alone, on the basis that He has no son." Al-Suddi also said: the meaning is, "If He had a son, I would be the first to worship Him, on the basis that He has a son, but that is not fitting." Al-Mahdawi said: "in" in these views is conditional, and this is the best view, and it is the choice of al-Tabari, because if it meant "ma," it could be taken to mean that He did not have a son in the past.

It was said: the meaning of "al-'Abidin" is "al-Anifin" (those who are disdainful). Some scholars said: if it were so, it would be "al-'Abidin" (with a short vowel), meaning: [the verse would read] "al-'Abidin."

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and al-Yamani also read "fa-ana awwalu al-'abidin" without the alif, from 'abida, ya'bidu, 'abadan (with a vowel on the middle letter), meaning he became disdainful and angry, so he is 'abid, and the noun is al-'abadah, like al-anafah (disdain), according to Abu Zayd. Al-Farazdaq said:

"Those are my companions, so bring me their like...
And I disdain to satirize Kulayb with Darim."

And another recites:

"Those are people who, if they satirize me, I satirize them...
And I disdain that Kulayb be satirized with Darim."

Al-Jawhari said: Abu 'Amr said, and God's saying "fa-ana awwalu al-'abidin" is from disdain and anger. Al-Kisa'i and al-Qutabi said likewise, as al-Mawardi related from them both. Al-Harawi said: His saying "fa-ana awwalu al-'abidin" is said to be from 'abida, ya'badu, meaning from the disdainful. Ibn 'Arafah said: it is only said 'abida, ya'badu, fa-huwa 'abid, and rarely is 'abid said. The Qur'an does not come with the rare of the language or the anomalous. Rather, the meaning is: "I am the first to worship God, Mighty and Majestic, as One who has no son."

It is narrated that a woman entered upon her husband and gave birth to a child from him after six months. This was mentioned to 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him, and he ordered her to be stoned. 'Ali said to him: God the Exalted said: ﴿And his carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15], and He said in another verse: ﴿And his weaning is in two years﴾ [Luqman: 14]. By God, 'Uthman did not disdain; he sent to her and she was returned.

'Abd Allah ibn Wahb said: he meant he did not feel disdain nor was he angry. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "fa-ana awwalu al-'abidin" means "al-ghidab al-anifin" (the angry, disdainful ones). It was also said: "fa-ana awwalu al-'abidin" means: I am the first to worship Him in unity, opposing you. Abu 'Ubaydah said: its meaning is "al-jahidin" (the deniers), and he related: "'abadani haqqi," meaning "jahadani" (he denied me). 

The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read "wuldun" with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam. The rest, and 'Asim, read "walad," and this has been discussed previously.

"Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth": meaning, exalted and sanctified above all. He declared Himself free of everything that implies createdness, and commanded the Prophet ﷺ to declare Him free of such things.

"Above what they describe": meaning, above what they say of falsehood.

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers.﴾ Its meaning has been disputed. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: the meaning is "There was not for the Most Merciful a son," so "in" (in) here means "ma" (not), the sentence is complete on this reading, and then one begins with "then I am the first of the worshippers," that is, the first of the monotheists among the people of Makkah, on the basis that He has no son. The pause on "al-'Abidin" (the worshippers) is complete. It was also said: the meaning is, "Say, O Muhammad, if it were established that God has a son, then I would be the first to worship His son, but it is impossible that He should have a son." This is like what you say to one you are debating: "If what you said is proven by evidence, then I am the first to believe it," which is an exaggeration in deeming it unlikely, meaning there is no way to believe it. This is a softening of speech, like His saying: ﴿And indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba: 24]. The meaning on this view is: "Then I am the first of the worshippers of that son, because honouring the son is honouring the father." Mujahid said: the meaning is, "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first to worship Him alone, on the basis that He has no son." Al-Suddi also said: the meaning is, "If He had a son, I would be the first to worship Him, on the basis that He has a son, but that is not fitting." Al-Mahdawi said: "in" in these views is conditional, and this is the best view, and it is the choice of al-Tabari, because if it meant "ma," it could be taken to mean that He did not have a son in the past.

It was said: the meaning of "al-'Abidin" is "al-Anifin" (those who are disdainful). Some scholars said: if it were so, it would be "al-'Abidin" (with a short vowel), meaning: [the verse would read] "al-'Abidin."

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and al-Yamani also read "fa-ana awwalu al-'abidin" without the alif, from 'abida, ya'bidu, 'abadan (with a vowel on the middle letter), meaning he became disdainful and angry, so he is 'abid, and the noun is al-'abadah, like al-anafah (disdain), according to Abu Zayd. Al-Farazdaq said:

"Those are my companions, so bring me their like...
And I disdain to satirize Kulayb with Darim."

And another recites:

"Those are people who, if they satirize me, I satirize them...
And I disdain that Kulayb be satirized with Darim."

Al-Jawhari said: Abu 'Amr said, and God's saying "fa-ana awwalu al-'abidin" is from disdain and anger. Al-Kisa'i and al-Qutabi said likewise, as al-Mawardi related from them both. Al-Harawi said: His saying "fa-ana awwalu al-'abidin" is said to be from 'abida, ya'badu, meaning from the disdainful. Ibn 'Arafah said: it is only said 'abida, ya'badu, fa-huwa 'abid, and rarely is 'abid said. The Qur'an does not come with the rare of the language or the anomalous. Rather, the meaning is: "I am the first to worship God, Mighty and Majestic, as One who has no son."

It is narrated that a woman entered upon her husband and gave birth to a child from him after six months. This was mentioned to 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him, and he ordered her to be stoned. 'Ali said to him: God the Exalted said: ﴿And his carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15], and He said in another verse: ﴿And his weaning is in two years﴾ [Luqman: 14]. By God, 'Uthman did not disdain; he sent to her and she was returned.

'Abd Allah ibn Wahb said: he meant he did not feel disdain nor was he angry. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "fa-ana awwalu al-'abidin" means "al-ghidab al-anifin" (the angry, disdainful ones). It was also said: "fa-ana awwalu al-'abidin" means: I am the first to worship Him in unity, opposing you. Abu 'Ubaydah said: its meaning is "al-jahidin" (the deniers), and he related: "'abadani haqqi," meaning "jahadani" (he denied me). 

The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read "wuldun" with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam. The rest, and 'Asim, read "walad," and this has been discussed previously.

"Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth": meaning, exalted and sanctified above all. He declared Himself free of everything that implies createdness, and commanded the Prophet ﷺ to declare Him free of such things.

"Above what they describe": meaning, above what they say of falsehood.

"The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So leave them to plunge into vain talk and to play﴾ — meaning the disbelievers of Makkah, when they denied the punishment of the Hereafter. That is: leave them to plunge into their falsehood and to play in their worldly life ﴿until they meet their Day which they are promised﴾, whether the punishment in this world or in the Hereafter. It has also been said: this is abrogated by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf, the verse of fighting). It has also been said: it is muhkam (fixed, not abrogated), and it was only stated in the form of a threat.

Ibn Muhaysin, Mujahid, Humayd, Ibn al-Qa'qa' and Ibn al-Sumaiqa' recited ﴿hatta yalqaw﴾ with a fatha on the ya' and a sukun on the lam, without an alif, and with a fatha on the qaf here, in (surat) al-Tur [[verse 45]] and al-Ma'arij [[verse 42]]. The rest recited ﴿yulaqu﴾."

This is a refutation of their claim that God has a partner and a son; that is, He is the one deserving worship in the heavens and on earth. ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) and others said: the meaning is "and He is the one who is in the heaven a god, and in the earth a god" [[In some copies of the original: "... fi al-sama' ilah wa fi al-ard ..."]], and he recited it accordingly. The meaning is that He is worshipped in both. It is also narrated that he, along with Ibn Mas'ud and others, recited "wa huwa alladhi fi al-sama' Allah wa fi al-ard Allah," and this is contrary to the Mushaf.

"Ilah" is in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "And He who is in the heaven is God," as stated by Abu ʿAli (Abu ʿAli al-Farisi). Its omission is acceptable because the sentence is long. It is also said that "fi" here carries the meaning of "ʿala" (on), as in His saying, ﴿And I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ta-Ha: 71], meaning "on the trunks of palm trees" [[See vol. 11, p. 224.]]. That is, He is the one capable over the heavens and the earth. "And He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing" has already been discussed [[See vol. 1, p. 287, second or third edition.]].

"Tabāraka" is from tafā'ala, from al-barakah (blessing; the form implies abundance and exaltation), and it has already been discussed [see vol. 7, p. 223].

"And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour," i.e., the time of its establishment.

"And to Him you will be returned" — Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa-ilayhi yurja'una" with the letter ya' (they will be returned). The rest read it with the letter ta' (you will be returned). Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, Ya'qub and Ibn Abi Ishaq used to open its first letter with fatha, according to their own principles (usul). The rest used damma.

It was discussed in the first point: Al-Qurtubi's commentary on verse 86 of Surah al-Zukhruf (43).

Qur'anic quotations and commentary:

**The first issue:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Except for those who testify to the truth﴾. The word "min" (مَنْ, "those who") is in the genitive position (fi mahall al-khafd). By "those who call upon besides Him" he meant Jesus, Ezra (Uzayr), and the angels. The meaning is: these beings do not possess intercession except for those who testify to the truth and believe with knowledge and insight. This was stated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others. He said: the testimony to the truth is "There is no god but Allah."

It was also said that "man" (مَنْ) is in the nominative position (fi mahall raf'), meaning: those who are called upon besides Him do not possess intercession, namely the deities, according to the view of Qatadah. That is, they do not intercede for their worshippers except those who testify to the truth, namely Ezra, Jesus, and the angels, for they testify to the truth and to the oneness of Allah. ﴿And they know﴾ the reality of what they testified to.

It was also said that the verse was revealed because al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and a group of Quraysh said: "If what Muhammad says is true, then we will take the angels as allies, and they are more deserving of intercession for us than he is." So Allah revealed: ﴿And those who call upon besides Him do not possess intercession, except he who testifies to the truth﴾. That is, they believed that the angels, or the idols, or the jinn, or the devils would intercede for them, but there is no intercession for anyone on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Except he who testifies to the truth﴾, meaning the believers, when permission is given to them.

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿Except he who testifies to the truth﴾, that is, one who testifies that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.

It was also said: the meaning is that these worshippers besides Allah do not possess for anyone the ability to intercede for them, except one who testifies to the truth, for whoever testifies to the truth may be interceded for, while no intercession is made for a polytheist. The word "illa" (إِلَّا) here means "but" (bi-ma'na lakin): that is, the polytheists do not obtain intercession, but whoever testifies to the truth obtains it. Thus it is an exceptive clause that is disjunctive (istithna' munqati'). It may also be connected (muttasil), because the phrase "those who call upon besides Him" includes the angels. It is said: "shafa'tuhu" and "shafa'tu lahu," like "kiltuhu" and "kiltu lahu." The meaning of intercession and its derivation was already covered in al-Baqarah, so there is no point in repeating it [[See vol. 1, p. 378 of the second or third edition.]].

It was also said: ﴿Except he who testifies to the truth﴾ means: except one for whom the angels testify that he was upon the truth in the world, with their knowledge of that from him, either because Allah informed them of it, or because they witnessed his faith.

**The second issue:** The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Except he who testifies to the truth, while they know﴾ indicates two meanings. The first: intercession based on truth is not beneficial unless accompanied by knowledge, and mere affirmation does not suffice without knowledge of the correctness of the statement. The second: the condition for all other testimonies concerning rights and other matters is that the witness must have knowledge of them. Similar to this is what is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "If you see something like the sun, then testify; otherwise, leave it." This was already discussed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 3, p. 389.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 43, verse 87:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created them?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ That is: they would certainly acknowledge that Allah created them after they had not been anything. "Then how are they turned away?" That is: how are they turned back from His worship and diverted from it, so that they associate others with Him, hoping for their intercession with Him? It is said: "afakahu, ya'fikuhu, afkan," meaning he turned him around and diverted him from something. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Have you come to us to turn us away from our gods?"﴾[[Verse 22 of Surah al-Ahqaf.]] [al-Ahqaf: 22]. It has also been said: that is, if you asked the angels and Jesus, "Who created them?" they would say, "Allah." "Then how are they turned away?" That is: how are these people turned away in their claim that those (beings) are gods?

In "qīlihi" (his saying) there are three readings: the accusative (naṣb), the genitive (jarr), and the nominative (raf'). The genitive is the reading of ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah. The rest of the seven readers read it in the accusative. The nominative is the reading of al-Aʿraj, Qatādah, Ibn Hurmuz, and Muslim ibn Jundub. Whoever reads it in the genitive takes it to mean: "And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour and the knowledge of his saying." Whoever reads it in the accusative takes it to mean: "And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and He knows his saying," and this is the view chosen by al-Zajjaj. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Akhfash said that "qīlihi" may be a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the words of God, ﴿that We do not hear their secret and their private talk﴾ [[Verse 80 of this surah. [Az-Zukhruf: 80]]]. Ibn al-Anbārī said: I asked Abū al-ʿAbbās Muḥammad ibn Yazīd al-Mubarrad, "On what basis do you put qīl in the accusative?" He said: "I put it in the accusative upon 'And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and He knows his saying.'" On this reading, it is not good to stop at "turjaʿūn" (you will be returned) or at "yaʿlamūn" (they know). It is good to stop at "yaktubūn" (they write) [[In verse 80.]]. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Akhfash also permitted putting it in the accusative on the sense: "We do not hear their secret and their private talk and his saying," as we have quoted from them. On this reading, it is not good to stop at "yaktubūn." Al-Farrāʾ and al-Akhfash also permitted that it be in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), as if he had said: "And he said his saying, and complained his complaint to God, Mighty and Majestic," as Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr said:

"The slanderers walk on their sides, and their saying: 'Indeed you, O son of Abī Sulmā, are to be killed.'"

He meant: "And they say their saying." As for whoever reads "qīlihi" in the nominative, the estimated construction is: "And with Him is his saying," or "His saying is heard," or "His saying is this statement" [[Or "his saying is this statement" is omitted in ḥ, and in z and l it reads "and in it this statement."]]. Al-Zamakhsharī said: What they have said is not strong in meaning, given the intervening of a separation between the conjunct and the conjoined by something that does not suit being a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ), and given the disharmony of the composition (naẓm). Stronger and more likely than that is that the genitive and the accusative are on the basis of an implied and omitted particle of oath (ḥarf al-qasam). The nominative is on the basis of their saying: "Ayman Allāh" (by the rights of God), "Amānat Allāh" (by the trust of God), "Yamīn Allāh" (by the oath of God), and "La-ʿamruka" (by your life). The words ﴿Indeed these are a people who do not believe﴾ would be the answer to the oath, as if he had said: "And he swore by his saying, O Lord, or 'his saying, O Lord, is my oath': indeed these are a people who do not believe." Ibn al-Anbārī said: In Arabic it is permissible to read "wa-qīlihi" in the nominative, by taking it as the subject of "Indeed these are a people who do not believe." Al-Mahdawī said: Or it may be on the estimate: "And his saying is: his saying, O Lord," so he omitted the second "qīlihi," which is the predicate (khabar), and the place of "O Lord" is in the accusative by the implied predicate. This is not impossible, since the omission of part of a relative construction while part of it remains is not permitted, because the omission of "qawl" (saying) has become so common that it is like something mentioned. The pronoun in "qīlihi" refers to ʿĪsā, and it is said that it refers to Muḥammad ﷺ, since his mention has preceded when He said ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 81]. Abū Qilābah read "yā Rabba" with a fatḥah on the bāʾ. Al-qīl is a verbal noun like al-qawl (saying), and from it comes the hadith: "He forbade qīl and qāl" [[The hadith is bracketed as it appears in the source.]]. It is said: "I said a saying (qawlan), and a qīlan, and a qālan." And in al-Nisāʾ: ﴿And who is more truthful than God in speech (qīlan)?﴾ [[Verse 122.]] [An-Nisāʾ: 122].

Qatada said: He was commanded to pardon them, then He commanded him to fight them, so the pardon was abrogated (mansukh) by the sword. Similar to this is what Ibn Abbas said: "So pardon them" means turn away from them. "And say, 'Peace'" means good words, i.e., say to the polytheists of Makkah, "But soon you will know." Then this was abrogated in Surat Bara'a (al-Tawbah) by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], and so on to the end of the verse. It was also said: it is muhkam (decisive) and was not abrogated. The recitation of the common readers is "fa-sawfa ya'lamun" (with the ya'), as a report from Allah, may He be exalted, to His Prophet, in the form of a threat. Nafi' and Ibn Amir read "ta'lamun" (with the ta'), as an address from the Prophet ﷺ to the polytheists, in the form of a threat. "Salam" is in the nominative by an implied "alaykum" (upon you), as said by al-Farra'. Its meaning is a command to bid them farewell with peace, and he did not make it a greeting to them, as related by al-Naqqash. Shu'ayb ibn al-Habhab related that he taught him, by this, how to greet them, and Allah knows best.
